utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, on behalf of Bruno Stojic, it's appropriate to start by saying - on behalf of the entire team - that it is a singular honour to appear before of Your Honours in this, the last appeal of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. This Court, when it was established, was a distant dream to many, and yet its contribution to the rule of law to facilitate peace and reconciliation and to cross-fertilise different legal systems with some fundamental principles is significant. The impact of this Court goes well beyond the Balkans, but it is only right there we start with the Balkans and start on behalf of Bruno Stojic with a word of sympathy to express our very sincerest condolences for all the people of the former Yugoslavia - whatever their race, religion, ethnicity, be they Croat, Serbian or Bosnian Muslims or any other ethnic or affiliated group - because they survived exceptionally dark days, perhaps the darkest days that Europe has seen since the Second World War; and their courage to survive and to continue deserves our respect. On behalf of Bruno Stojic, we give it without reservation. One cannot help but be moved when we see the photographs like the Prosecution put up yesterday of the Dretelj camp. When one sees photographs like that, there is - understandably - a visceral reaction of abhorrence that man can make his fellow man, woman, and child still suffer. But, Your Honour, we're not - and this Tribunal and this appeal - is not focussed as some outpouring of grief. The focus of the trial was contained within the four walls of the indictment, whether or not the Prosecution had proved the case it put forward. And in this appeal, Your Honours, of course, the task for Your Honours is to determine the respective merits of the Defence appeals and the Prosecution responses within the prism of Article 25. We say that there are ample grounds to show that both there are manifest mistakes, which have occasioned a miscarriage of justice, and numerous errors of law which invalidate the decision. The Prosecution are the architects essentially of this case. They chose the scope of this case. They chose the mode of liability of joint criminal enterprise. Almost 18 years ago - there's a certain symmetry in this case - almost 18 years in the very first appeal of this Tribunal, the Tadic decision, the Judges rendered a decision on JCE. This is the last opportunity for the Judges to consider it against the evidence and against the facts. It is well known - it needs no repetition - that the doctrine itself, particularly the form of joint criminal enterprise 3, has around -- aroused significant controversy. It has not been followed by the International Criminal Court. It has been rejected by the ECCC. Importantly, I think, because going back to Nuremburg and the Control Council 10 and subsequent proceedings and the genesis of joint enterprise, the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom in the case of Jogee last year very boldly; courageously, I would submit; and very appropriately announced that it made a misstep back in 1985. Your Honours, we haven't in our brief sought to persuade Your Honours to revisit the contours of joint criminal enterprise. What we say is that according to the law as it stands, as articulated in Your Honours' jurisprudence in Brdjanin and others, the Chamber ran into error. Your Honour, this appeal has many aspects, but one of the features is whether or not the elements have really been satisfied beyond reasonable doubt; whether or not the joint criminal enterprise in this case - the massive, extensive, far-reaching joint criminal enterprise - can be proved and has been proved by way of a properly reasoned decision based upon inferences from circumstantial evidence. Because there's no direct evidence of a joint criminal enterprise; it is inferences woven together. Your Honour, we rely fully on our brief that we have submitted, the 52 grounds, I think it was, that are contained in our brief which are fully referenced. In the time allotted to me today, I'm going to endeavour to deal with three main themes, if I get there. The first is the Defence argument that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that there was a joint criminal enterprise of the type it found. The second limb is that even if they were correct that there was a joint criminal enterprise, they erred in fact and in law in finding that Bruno Stojic was part of that joint criminal enterprise. And the last limb, if I get to it, will be some submissions regarding the expanded JCE. It is not without significance, perhaps, Your Honours, that right at the beginning of volume 4, the majority's decision, they announce in paragraph 41, and I quote: "The Prosecution alleges the existence of several JCEs set up at various times and under various forms. However, as will be set forth below, the Chamber considers that the evidence demonstrates that there was only one, single common criminal purpose - domination by the HZ-HB Croats through ethnic cleansing of the Muslim population." In that paragraph, if one pauses for a moment, Your Honours may gain an insight into the some of the challenges and some of the difficulties that we say have become manifest in the course of this judgement. The majority - rather ambitiously you may think - decided rather than to go with the Prosecution's assertion of several JCEs, they would posit that there is one massive overarching joint criminal enterprise. Your Honour, lest there be any suggestion, we - on behalf of Bruno Stojic - do not ascribe any conspiracy to the majority. We do not say that they have approached this mala fides or with any ulterior intent. Both Judge Trechsel and Judge Prandler are eminent jurists, honourable individuals. But the fact remains that we assert vigorously that they had fallen into error. Human frailty is something that attaches to each and every one of us. So, Your Honour, it may that the majority was simply overwhelmed and couldn't handle a massive case of the type alleged by the Prosecution; and in their attempt to make sense of the disparate information, the masses of documents put forward by all parties, they sought evidence - instinctively perhaps, but erroneously - that fitted their -- the theory they decided upon. Because however one dices it, however one looks at it, the fact remains that very critical evidence has not been considered by the majority. And I will come back to that, if I may. Your Honours, if -- at this point I would seek to hand up - I've already given it to the court usher - short skeletons in relation to the questions raised by Your Honours and that's fully footnoted. I think that will help us move a little bit quickly. It may also help the Prosecution because some of those questions will be dealt with next week, so it will give them a bit more time. But perhaps those can be distributed, one for each of the Judges and for the Prosecution, and for the -- our colleagues as well. Your Honour, while that's being done, I will move straight to the first contention that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have not obviously had a chance to review this but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: But it does like a mini-brief actually, so we would object to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the purpose, of course, of the hearing is to get to the truth and to allow Your Honours as much clarity as possible. We've organised it every question has a new page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We are all agreed here - and thank you for being patient with us - we see absolutely nothing wrong with following this procedure. These are submissions that are being made by appellant -- Mr. Kahn in response to the questions that we have indicated in our 1st March order. So basically this is not part of the evidence; it's an aid that the Defence is providing us in order to speed up and also follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm most grateful for that kindness. Your Honour, as is apparent, the JCE encompasses both individuals that had died at the time the case -- the indictment was brought, President Tudjman, Bobetko, and Susak. It comprised both political leaderships in the form of Boban, Mr. Prlic, and Mr. Stojic; and the military in terms of Praljak -- General Praljak and General Petkovic and other members of the HVO. The time duration was 16 months, 21 different crimes alleged within that alleged joint criminal enterprise, and - as Your Honour, Mr. President noted yesterday - dealt with a broad geographic area, eight municipalities and five detention centres. The scale is not the complaint. We can understand and accept that joint criminal enterprise -- in fact, maybe its greatest utility is in a wide case, but it has some implications in our respectful submission. Because the wider the JCE, the more the temptation perhaps to find -- greater the danger, perhaps, to find the existence of a JCE without satisfying each and every essential element that is required in that doctrine to prevent it becoming such a ill-disciplined concept that certainty in the law is completely eviscerated. Your Honour, as mentioned, there's no direct evidence of an agreement between the alleged members of the JCE, and that's why I said at the outset this case is based upon inferences and whether or not the inferences that the Prosecution put forward and which the Trial Chamber considered were the only reasonable inferences open to that Trial Chamber. I can fully accept that certain dots were joined by the Trial Chamber and a certain picture emerged which finds form particularly in the decision of the majority. But we say that the picture that emerged by the Judges, the majority, joining those dots only emerged because they failed to consider many other dots on the board, which - if they had considered - would have displayed a very different landscape. Your Honour, with your collective experience as a Bench, knowing the Balkans, and seeing the briefs of the parties, it is clear that the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia in the period of the indictment were not clear-cut; they were fast-changing, they were complex, they were contradictory, and perhaps immediately a red flag should be raised. Because when in that complexity a nice little package of a concept is articulated, either it could be absolutely accurate or it could amount to a gross simplification; we say that it was the latter. Dealing with Ground 1, really, the foundations of the case we say - and it's on your screens, Your Honours - that the extract of the Judgement that is displayed shows a sweeping finding. The majority referred to leaders of the HZ(R)HB - pause there for a moment - fails anywhere in the judgement to define who these leaders of the HZ(R)HB are. But what it finds, what the majority finds, is that all times of the indictment, whatever the political situation, whatever the pressure from Serbia, whatever the pressure from the international community, whatever negotiations were ongoing, there was a complete consistency as far as the ultimate purpose is concerned. Well, Your Honour, there's no Northern Star to guide the majority; there was the evidence. And it's important when looking at paragraph 24 of the judgment, that the majority's conclusion is clearly based primarily on the intentions of one man - not Bruno Stojic, our client - but the intentions that were attributed to president Franjo Tudjman. And in the 24 paragraphs of the Judgement, it's noticeable that, whereas there's many mentions of president Tudjman and others, there's only squeezed in - gratuitously perhaps for the Prosecution - squeezed in is one mention, one solitary mention, of Bruno Stojic. One of the characteristics when one is assessing this ground of appeal are the presidential transcripts; they loom large. And significant weight must be given to those transcripts because they are an almost verbatim recording of private conversations between certain actors that are relevant to the Prosecution's case and the leadership in Croatia. And they are particularly relevant, given the finding by the majority, that the position of President Tudjman, who stands astride this judgment like a colossus, that his position was - in their words - that he spoke equivocally, that in public everything was fine and dandy, peace and love to all, support for Bosnia. But the majority say that in private a very different picture emerges of a veracious leader who to wishes to dismember a neighbouring state. Well, Your Honour, this is why our ground for appeal is so important because if that is right as a matter -- as a reasonable inference available to the Judges - give weight to the private recordings, innermost conversations, innermost feelings, no spin, no audience outside the inner circle - then it was mandatory for those Judges in discharging their oath and to assess fairly the case to consider all of the presidential transcripts that were relevant to this issue and they failed, patently failed, to do that. When one considers those presidential transcripts that we refer to in our brief, it is clear that there is no double game being played at all. There's a complex situation, and complexity sometimes has to be simply acknowledged, particularly in a court of law. Inconvenient facts, events that don't square cannot be brushed under the carpet or put to one side; they need to be confronted head on, and - as we'll see in our brief and hopefully I'll show - that the majority failed to do. Your Honour, in assessing all of those transcripts, the Defence do not have to prove that President Franjo Tudjman was a great humanitarian. We do not have to prove that he didn't at any point of encourage Croatian intervention in Bosnia. We don't have to prove that he never wavered in what he was thinking at any moment in time. The only thing we have to establish is that no reasonable Chamber, properly considering the evidence, could have found this ambitious, overarching, never wavering, ultimate purpose that the majority hinged their decision upon. Your Honour, when it comes to the presidential transcripts, I would invite Your Honours to give significant weight to the very forensically detailed approach of Judge Antonetti, the President of that Trial Chamber. Your Honour, Judges can render decisions to greater claim. They can render decisions that are criticised, even vehemently, but to steal the words of Kipling, Judges are well advised to "treat those two imposters of triumph and disaster just the same." When it comes to Your Honours' assessment of the merits of Judge Antonetti's dissent and findings, we humbly pray that you confine yourself - as we're sure you will - to the covers of volume 6; and decide, when viewing that volume 6 against the evidence, whether or not Judge Cassese's -- Judge Antonetti's findings were reasonable and justified and supported by chapter and verse. Because if Your Honours find, as we would urge you to do so, when it comes to the treatment of the presidential transcripts, that Judge Antonetti's findings are absolutely reasonable and absolutely correct, it would irresistibly follow that the conclusions of the majority is not -- as being the only possible inferences is unsound, and I think that must follow as night from day. Your Honour, all the references are in our briefs, but if I could perhaps put on the screen P00822, and you'll see from that at page 52 that this is a portion of a presidential transcript dated 27th of November, 1992, inner-most sanctum, the Croatian Defence and National Security Council - no need to cloak the true intentions of President Tudjman. And what he says in relation to the Bosnian Muslims is on the screen: "We should thus endeavour that our people in Bosnia and Herzegovina do not breach that general agreement and that a political and military co-operation be established in this war, even if [sic] we do things in their favour even when they have not completely earned it." And he continued. Speaking between ourselves, he's very revealing speaking amongst this trusted group that were around him: "If it is possible to hold Bosnia and Herzegovina together as a community of three constituent peoples in which the Croatian people will have their position secured [sic], let it be held together. But if it cannot be held together, if the world, Europe and America let [sic] the Serbs take their areas, let the Muslims come with us, let the Croatian interests be secured in this [sic] way." Well, the first thing, nothing about ethnic cleansing. Nothing about, God forbid, Muslims being untouchables, to be kept away. Let the Muslims come with us, completely contrary to the majority's finding. And this is just two months before the majority find the JCE started in January 1993. Your Honour, it shows understandably that the aim was, of course, as you'd expect from a leader, the interests of his own country, namely, Croatia and to ensure ideally keeping Bosnia together. Of course, alternative scenarios are discussed. Well, which leader wouldn't discuss contingencies at a time when the world held its breath looking at the scenes that were visited as upon our television screens as Bosnia was in crisis, and nobody knew if that republic would be recognised or survive at all. But it cannot be said that these documents from the presidential transcript show an ultimate aim to reconstitute the Banovina of 1939. The Judges, the majority, completely failed to address this document; they turned away from it. An inconvenient truth, perhaps. Something that was too difficult to handle because it was at odds with their overarching ultimate aim, JCE, which they found. Your Honour, it's true when one looks at our brief that President Tudjman's interest in an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina through a confederate model is apparently in various presidential transcripts, but the Trial Chamber - whilst citing some of those transcripts - found that President Tudjman "continued to be preoccupied with the borders of Croatia and the Croatian Banovina." But that's not the only inference. That's not the only reasonable inference. That's what's critical for Your Honours. That's not the only reasonable inference that can be ascribed to those transcripts and that evidence. It's consistent with a desire to protect his country, Croatia. It's consistent with a desire to avoid economic sanctions, to defend his territory and the territory of Croatia and the interests of Croatian people, whilst ensuring he was compliant with what the rest of the world was demanding. It's equally consistent with an unable desire to prevent a Greater Croatia coming right to the -- a Greater Serbia coming to the border. Your Honour, we can put on the screen now P1883 and page 12. April -- 15th of April, 1993. Again, a document not considered. Four months after the JCE is said to have been hatched and in operation by the majority, and President Tudjman says that the Americans envisaged co-operation as best relations with the Muslims as possible, which is of course what we are doing. If the majority are correct that gives significant weight to these private conversations as evidence of the real intentions of the protagonist in those meetings, why look away from this in which President Tudjman is saying it's not about getting rid of Bosnia-Herzegovina but doing their best to have good relations with the Muslims. P2466 at page 11 you have another example. 20th of May, 1993, five months after the alleged JCE was found by the majority in that impugned decision. And President Tudjman says and I quote: "I informed them, the Croatian representatives in the context of Mostar, that by leading the politics of escalation of conflict with Muslim, they are endangering the interests of the Croatian state because of the indication of sanctions." Now, Your Honour, in each transcript different issues are in the forefront of the mind of President Tudjman, different issues are being discussed; but they do not show a preoccupation in our respectful submissions with the borders of Croatia. They refer to co-operation and the reality that escalation was against Croatia's interest for many obvious reasons. And all of these transcripts are contrary to the JCE put forward by the Prosecution and embraced wholeheartedly and vigorously by the majority of the Trial Chamber. Now, the Prosecution will say, Well, it's all about avoiding sanctions. He may have responded in that ilk when he was trying to do a sidestep and avoid sanctions. Well, we say that's not a convincing answer. It's a lame answer. It is an unconvincing answer. Because of course every head of state, every leader would like to avoid sanctions. But the desire to avoid sanctions is completely - if he was honest about it - is completely contradictory with the theory of the Prosecution that Tudjman wished to divide up Bosnia in breach of what the rest of the world wanted at the time. Of course, there would be consequences. Of course, there would be repercussions. And of course it would be readily foreseeable, if not absolutely certain, there would be sanctions. So how to the Prosecution square that paradox? They don't. How do the majority deal with it? They don't deal with the document at all. Your Honours, alternative inferences, alternative readings are contained not only in the presidential transcripts, but in the submissions we put forward, including that the establishment of the HVO must be seen in the context of a legitimate need to defend the Croatian people and the people in those areas of all ethnicities from aggression, that unfortunately Serbia at that time was engaged, the government and paramilitaries of Serbia. And that argument - and it staggers belief - that argument, that important argument, was not cited by the majority in its summary of Defence submissions. The way the majority dealt with that argument of us, of the Defence, is at paragraph 15 of the Judgement. And they say that: "Although HZ-HB was created against a backdrop of war in response to Serb aggression ... the various components of BiH population may have believed it was their right to organise themselves in order to secure their own survival ..." Well, that's strange. I think the first right of every human being is to defend themselves for their survival; there's no equivocation necessary. But, Your Honour, what do they then go on to say? They observed that Franjo Tudjman was advocating the existence and legitimacy of the BiH Croatian people in order to protect the borders of Croatia. Well, we say that that's a very curious way of avoiding the pressing issue. The Chamber acknowledged HZ-HB was created against a backdrop of war. They acknowledged that components, the peoples in that area, were trying to organise themselves for their survival. But through reference to what they contend to be one man's desire to recreate the Banovina, they say all of those actions, all of those steps, all of that organisation was simply pursuant to an ultimate objective. It's ludicrous. It's far too simplistic. And it doesn't do justice to the complexity, the factual complexity that one has to struggle with to do justice in this case. In fact, Your Honours, a legitimate response to Serbian aggression in those times, in that context, looking at the evidence before the Chamber was absolutely a reasonable alternative way of reading many of the events cited by the majority. Why always cling on to the overarching ultimate aim, JCE? Neat, tidy, attractive at first blush, but not consistent with the facts. Your Honour, the formation of the HVO was an important step in the -- in the region - and it's set out at paragraph 25 of the second amended indictment - that the HVO was one of the essential structures and instruments of the JCE. And we can put P151 on the screen, which makes it clear - if one looks at it fairly, dispassionately, objectively - that the aim of the HVO was created in order to protect the Croatian people, not as a homogeneous, pure race of people, protect the Croatian people as well as other people in this community attacked by the aggressor. And it is very clear from the documents, the aggressor that's being referred to at that period are the Serbs. So nothing about ethnic cleansing, nothing about ultimate purpose; it's about organising to protect the people living in that area, in that geographical area, that was dominated numerically by the Croatians, by the Croats of Herceg-Bosna. Not discriminatory at all. Your Honour, there is a lot of documents in the brief, there's a lot of documents that are in the appellate briefs of our learned friends. But we say, with the greatest of respect, that the majority have engaged in a thesis that perhaps is more appropriate for a historian than a Judge. The luxury of giving colour to certain inferences and certain events and postulating an historical thesis, rather than Judges who must decide a case whether liberty of the accused is at stake to the criminal standard of beyond reasonable doubt. And it requires a candour to accept that the devil is in the detail, that things do not always -- they're not always as simple or as neat as one would like. And to confront those difficult pieces of evidence that don't fit the theory and then to explain them, not to ignore them. And, Your Honour, we say that when one considers these findings on Ground 1, it is really manifestly clear that the Judges embarked upon a very ambitious project in finding this creation of the Banovina being the ultimate aim and one that is simply not -- that doesn't comport with the facts and one would that only stand up to scrutiny if you ignore many of the presidential transcripts, a couple of which I've put on the screen today. They cannot, we say, fairly, in fairness to the fair trial rights of Mr. Stojic, be dealt with in not just that dismissive manner, but to be completely ignored in the manner that they have been in the majority's decision. Your Honour, the second point I'll move to is Ground 2, and that's the majority's finding that a common pattern of criminal conduct established a common purpose. And we say in Ground 2 that that decisively contradicted by the co-operation between the HVO and the armija. Now I really would ask Your Honours to give the most anxious scrutiny to our submissions in relation to this ground as well. A significant plank of our defence, not in closing, not today, but from the beginning of the trial was that the co-operation between the HVO and the armija helped show that the intent the Prosecution contended existed, the JCE that they asserted simply was untenable. That argument was one of only four arguments, four submissions that we put in our closing brief, one of only four. It contained 15 pages of our final brief. I made submissions on this issue in oral arguments, closing speeches. Six of our 19 witnesses, almost one-third, six of our 19 witness, Milos Cehulic, Pinju, Majic, Bahto, Makar spoke to that issue. Many documents were tendered in support of this proposition. Many more documents would have been tendered but for the -- what we say is the wholly erroneous and unfair decision of the majority to refuse to admit other documents, and that's dealt with in Ground 5. So on any measure, by any yard-stick, a very important plank, in fact the bedrock of our case. How did the majority deal with that? What should be expected? You will be staggered, Your Honours, they didn't. They didn't deal with those arguments at all. A reader examining the Trial Chamber's findings wouldn't know that this had been such a pivotal part of Defence submissions. It's not mentioned, these arguments are not mentioned in black and white in the analysis of JCE. Paragraph 39 of volume 4 is the single paragraph in the majority which is supposed to summarise the six arguments of the various Defence teams. That doesn't contain any mention of those witnesses or these arguments. It is telling, we say exceptionally revealing, that footnote 112 to that paragraph cites paragraphs 64 to 152 of our final brief, the Stojic final brief at trial. But this issue was addressed in paragraphs 34 to 63 of the final brief, not considered at all. Absolutely unreasonable. And these constitute by itself, we say, grounds for reversing the decision. The only objective conclusion is this important evidence, these important witnesses, a third of our Defence witnesses, a quarter of our submissions on common purpose were completely and utterly disregarded by the majority. We can put on the screen paragraph 440. The only finding dealing with this body of evidence is in volume 1, paragraph 440. And that, according to its subheading, deals with the period February 1992 to August 1992. But, Your Honour, the factual finding there is significant anyway, because the majority did not return to consider the implications of that finding when considering the common plan, whether or not a common plan existed. Surely they should have -- once they've said that there was co-operation between the HVO and armija against the JNA and it continued to early 1993, the next step there in that section -- or, of course, one would expect in the JCE section is to discuss and weigh and evaluate whether or not that co-operation impacted on the intent and the existence of the JCE at all. They didn't. Glossed over it. And it becomes more pronounced when one looks at, for example, the transcript of Mile Akmadzic, 17th June 2008, and that's the transcript at page 294 -- 294431 [sic]. And the evidence cited in support of that testimony at footnote 1038 of the majority included this testimony. So the majority decision cites Mile Akmadzic, and it referred to 1D01282, and we can go to that. The date of the document is May 1993. So the footnote that the testimony -- the testimony contains a reference to an exhibit. The date of the exhibit is May 1993, and one can see both in that text and down below a few lines later, mention of May 1993 and then later 29th of April, 1993. Hardly early 1993. So you get the position that even assessed against its own footnotes, the majority decision falls into disarray. Because even the footnotes it decides to then choose don't support the inference that supply, arms, munitions, gun, rockets continue until only early 1993. Your Honour, if the Judges had done what we had hoped of them, what we say was required of them, they would have, in fact, found that the co-operation, the MTS, the military arm support, logistic assistance, fire-arms, rockets continued throughout 1993. That's what a reasonable Trial Chamber would have done and that was amply supported by the evidence, 2D00229. These are just examples to show how fundamentally erroneous, how unsubstantial was the decision of the majority. Now, this document that's on the screen shows a letter from Arif Pasalic to Sefer Halilovic dated the 26th of February, 1993, and it states that until now, that's February -- end of February 1993, Safet Orucevic, he's from the 4th Corps of the armija had successfully performed major jobs regarding the entrance of goods with the HVO. So it clearly shows there's assistance and co-operation in February. Next document, 2D0031, 30th of March, so two months after the supposed commencement of the JCE. Your Honours, please pause for a moment and look at that document. 3 million bullets, 3.000 AK-47 assault riffs, 180 RPG rocket-launchers, 4.270 RPG mines, 30.625 kilograms of TNT provided to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Really? A joint criminal enterprise? Giving guns that can be turned upon oneself? Or is it support that runs counter to heart of the Prosecution's case that was erroneously accepted and ambitiously modified by the majority. Your Honour, let's go even further from March. Let's go to May. 2D01107. HVO Main Staff approved further materiels and equipment to the armija. And Makar Andjelko gave evidence about this transfer, and I'll just read the reference. It's his testimony in court of the 23rd of March, 2009, transcript 38.448 at lines 2 to 4. And he is the assistant Chief of Staff of the armija of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 2nd Corps. So he is a Bosnian army officer, senior, and he goes to Mostar and he collects in May - five months after this conjured-up JCE, we say - 600.000 rounds of ammo, of ammunition, and 2.000 rockets for rocket-propelled grenades and 200 assault rifles and 30 rocket-launchers. And the Prosecution say, Well -- they may say it's irrelevant because those weapons are to fight the Serbs. This is twisted, we say - I apologise, but it's twisted, contorted, and wholly expedient thinking by the Prosecution because they are arms that are mobile. You don't give an assault rifle or a weapon and say, It must stay there; it's tethered, it's anchored to the ground. Once you give to your opponent, a belligerent to a conflict, the people one is trying to destroy according to the Prosecution, of course you know those guns have no loyalty to the giver. They will fire just as well on the giver as anybody else. So is this something the Trial Chamber should have considered? They didn't. And look at the date and look at the location. May, Mostar. And it's only days importantly, it is only days before the fighting between the HVO and the armija escalated in Mostar itself. But all of that was apparently of any relevance to the majority. And again it's important, when one is assessing what happened in Mostar, was it a local reaction, escalations, as Judge Antonetti found between different egos and different personalities and chaos, is that more realistic, is that more believable; or is the only reasonable conclusion beyond reasonable doubt that it was all done pursuant to this ambitious overarching JCE? Your Honour, but there's more. Witnesses gave evidence that co-operation and provision MTS continued throughout the war. Now, Mario Milos, whose evidence wasn't cited by the Trial Chamber, T38657, highlighted - it's there - that throughout 1993 when Judge Antonetti asked him -- Judge Antonetti asked throughout 1993 were -- or did Croatia deliver weapons and munitions to the armija? And the answer was yes. And, Your Honour, here just referred in testimony to 2D00959, now that was a document dated August 1993 which we say was wrongly excluded by the majority. It was a document from August 1993 showing further MTS being given by HVO to the armija. But, Your Honour, Milos was not alone. Because when one goes to another very senior, very courageous officer, a General Hamid Bahto of the armija of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He said very much the same thing, and his evidence wasn't considered by the Chamber at all when it comes to a JCE and the provision -- the relevance of the provision of MTS to JCE. He is quoted only by the majority in mitigation. So they completely missed the point. We didn't bring this witness - as our brief attests - as somehow mitigation, that we have a Bosnian Muslim officer saying that some goodies were given to the armija. We brought these witnesses to show that the provision of such support, logistics, and weapons is completely opposite to the contended ultimate purpose JCE that was postulated by the Prosecution and General Hamid Bahto says at the transcript, page 39731 at line 17, that the alliance, and I quote: "Existed throughout the war. We were receiving technical and military assistance from Croatia throughout the war." So, Your Honour, I could go on and on and on, but time doesn't permit me. And, Your Honour, as is apparent in our brief, it wasn't just military equipment and hardware and rockets and guns that can kill and maim; it was logistical support, it was training in Croatia, it was hospitals in Croatia, it was armija, Bosnian army, logistical centres in Croatia. All of that just an irrelevance as far as the majority is concerned. And the joint commissions, the joint commands that had been established in 1993 between the armija and the HVO in Gornji Vakuf, in Central Bosnia, in Konjic disregard -- these were not areas where -- these were not areas where there were joint operations against the Serbs. So the fact of these joint commissions was not -- was that not evidentially significant? We say of course it was, and any reasonable Trial Chamber who properly mastered the facts and who properly managed to understand and distill those facts would have considered them and wouldn't have come to what we say was the wholly erroneous finding of the majority. 2D00150, and I'll deal with this quite quickly because I'm lagging quite behind. These documents show that as of the 9th of June, 1993, so six months after the JCE, and last column it shows the percentage of Muslims in various HVO units. Some units have more than 50 per cent Muslims, 50 per cent as of June, six months later. So was this assessed and properly understood reasonably as the only reasonable inference that somehow this would link in to the ultimate purpose? It wasn't. Now, the numbers dropped significantly from the 30th of June. Why? Was it because of an ultimate purpose that was hatched in January or was it because on that date HVO units themselves that contained Bosnian Muslim members turned against their comrades? Which -- which is more -- which is more reasonable? Yes, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I thought I said that. Your Honour, the attack of the Tihomir Misic barracks is important. When assessing all of this, it's easy to be critical. It was mammoth case to preside over, it was a mammoth case to render a judgement over. Your Honours will feel some sympathy with the Herculean task that confronted the Judges. I think all of us on all sides, Prosecution and Defence, struggle with the breadth and weight of this case; it's not easily digestible. But, Your Honour, this is not a majority missing one or two documents. It's missing what I would say is the foundation, one of the main pillars of a Defence case. And, Your Honour, this wasn't a short judgment. We have six volumes. It's very difficult to bring it to court. The majority is 1800 pages. It dwarfs even "War and Peace" at 1200 pages. It wasn't judicial economy of space that made them leave out this important evidence. It wasn't want of time. Because, as Mr. Karnavas said yesterday, Their Honours very properly, I don't criticise, took a lot of time, years, to consider this decision. But having given themselves all the time in the world and having given them all the space in the world, they missed the most important argument in the world for Mr. Bruno Stojic. Your Honours, the Prosecution may say, Well, it doesn't matter that a quarter of the submissions were rejected; they were useless. They're not relevant. But we say that that evidence decisively - it wasn't hyperbole - we say it decisively undermines the inference that there was a JCE. If Croatia and the HVO wished to partition the Bosnia-Herzegovina in that manner, it made no sense to give that type of weapons and that type of support to one's enemies. That's common sense we would submit. And Your Honour, going back to General Bahto again at transcript 37910 at lines 22 to 23, he said very clearly when he was asked in evidence, he said: "I couldn't possibly imagine that we were enemies." He is the senior Bosnian army officer. He couldn't imagine at all that we were enemies. And yet the JCE mantra remains. It's a nice case. It's a large case. It allows big fish who were not indicted while they were alive in the form of President Tudjman and Boban and others to appear as ghosts in these proceedings, but for the Defence they are phantoms to fight and they're very difficult to confront. And the way the case has been adjudicated really falls beneath the standard, we say, that -- well, meets the standard of appellant review to be reversed. Your Honour, I must move on. There is quite a bit more I could say on that topic. But moving on to Grounds 3 and 4, the clear pattern. The Judges in volume 4, in paragraphs 44 to 65 narrate what appears to be a very logical, progressive escalates in the conflict that brokers only one explanation, organise, planning, ultimate purpose joint criminal enterprise. But we say that picture emerges very beautifully from the pages only because the alternative - equally plausible, if not more plausible reality - is ignored, the fact there were flash-points. There were flash-points between men with guns, and that's what it was, it was the armija and the HVO, men with guns, former Yugoslavia disintegrating, different egos as Judge Antonetti mentioned, different local aims and proclivities, and flash-points. And as Judge Antonetti asked in his dissent and I quote: "Are we not confronted with a classic internal conflict while local political aspirations, the egos of some, and political ambition led to unmanageable situations in terms of authority and command." With the greatest of respect, I say the Judge hit the nail on the head. And seen in that light, the events narrated by the majority seem to show a pattern simply because those events and those facts that don't fit that pattern are not mentioned. And the issue also, we say, isn't whether or not a particular activity is offensive or defensive. It's whether or not each engagement is linked to the ultimate purpose of the joint criminal enterprise. And that's what the Judges should have done. In relation to each engagement, don't just focus on whether it's offensive or defensive, but say whether or not that particular engagement hailed back to the joint criminal purpose. We can put on screen perhaps paragraph 46. And this is Gornji Vakuf, starting in January 1993, leaders participating in peace talks and it talks about the attacks the HVO launched on the 18th of January. This finding, we say, is manifestly unreasonable. Why? Because it overlooks the reality in the record that these tensions didn't just suddenly descend from hell on the 18th of January, but there had been conflicts predating that. Was that discussed? And those engagements, those conflicts, those engagements with the armija were not - the Judges said - attributable to a JCE; but yet, the 18th of January event is said to be evidence of a JCE. Does it make sense really as the only plausible explanation? But particularly when you looked at the fact that that engagement was resolved, that conflagration was resolved after only a few days after the commencement of the JCE, without the HVO taking over the entire province. Well, the Prosecution will say, Well, the HVO had won some territory. Well, yes they did. But if there was a JCE to take over the Banovina and they're on a role, why not take over the whole of the territory? That was their aim, that was their ultimate purpose, the cat was out of the bag. There was an invasion, according to the Prosecution. Why not take over the Banovina? Why pause? We say that there was no transformative event that is cited by the majority that will distinguish the attack on the 18th of January as part of a JCE, and yet the attack on the same villages, same towns, on the 11th of January as not being part of a JCE. Now, the Prosecution seem to be recent converts to the idea that the 15th of January, 1993, amounts to a transformative event. Well, when on earth was that conversion on the road to The Hague? Because in their final trial brief at paragraph 8, they contested -- they contended that it was April 1992. So we say no transformative event at all. Your Honour, going to -- while I'm on Jablanica and -- sorry, on Gornji Vakuf, Your Honours have asked some questions regarding the nature and the attack. Your Honour, those answers are in our skeleton at page 7, and I'd refer them to you. But, Your Honours, the Prosecution contended yesterday in their submissions that it's clear-cut that a tank targeted a house and caused deaths. That was their response effectively - they said it was clear-cut - and that the evidence was clear that it was a tank, that people were not only killed when a shell hit the building, but also that people kept on firing. Well, Your Honour, the Prosecution have made their arguments at trial. We're looking at the appellate situation. What did actually the Judges find? Firstly, in clear and unequivocal terms, one would expect the Prosecution to say and accept that the Judges fell into legal error because they predicated their decision on the basis that shelling per se is indiscriminate. And that's as basic a legal error as one can get. The majority said weapons, more specifically shells, the nature of which is such that it is impossible to distinguish from civilian targets. That was their foundational finding. Wrong. And then, of course, there's no discussion by the majority as to the type of weapon; the accuracy of the weapon, the ordnance used; the proximity of the legitimate military targets to the house. There's no discussion of that. In fact, what there is in the evidence clearly is there is intelligence reports that were not contested that were received by the HVO that there was a bunker just before the house, close to the house. And the Prosecution's contention - well, there's smoke coming from a chimney, because there's smoke from a chimney there must be civilians - is really stretching it, we say, particularly when their witness Andrew Williams accepted that in the same area, on the same occasions, he knew that armija soldiers or people defending villages were firing from houses. No evidence that the house was marked with any symbol to say it's a protected place. We know, contrary to the Prosecution, that their witnesses said trenches were dug. We know from their witnesses that they said fighting started at 7.00 a.m. and the shelling took place at 12.00. So it's not some kind of uncontested civilian zone. There were soldiers fighting in the area that were significantly organised enough according to the time-frame, 7.00 till 12.00, to keep the HVO at bay until the shell was fired. But Andrew Williams is asked point blank by the Prosecution about if it's a tank and he repeatedly says: It's either a tank or an anti-tank missile. He doesn't confirm that it's a tank. And if one goes to volume 2, I think it's page 87, it's quite interesting -- well, if one goes to page 88, in relation to Gornji Vakuf at paragraph 348, the Judges talk about -- well, the Chamber notes, and I quote: "That the evidence shows in relation to Gornji Vakuf the HOV used tanks, artillery, rockets, and mobile anti-tank guns." Do they make that finding in relation to the question posed by Your Honours in relation to Dusa? Well, let's go to paragraph 357. The Chamber notes: "Villages were attacked with mortar shells, heavy machine-guns and artillery." Conspicuous by its absence is any mention of tanks. So the Prosecution contention is cherry-picking. Because it's also interesting that when one looks at the testimony of Kemal Sljivo and the Judges say at paragraph 344 that they give credence, not that they accept unequivocally or without reservation, they gave credence to the testimony of victims testifying, namely, Kemal Sljivo, witnesses testifying before the Chamber. It's important to note that witness never testified before the Chamber. That witness never testified before the Chamber, as is contended in paragraph 344. That was a 92 bis witness, not cross-examined. A belligerent to a conflict, fighting the people that are on the side of my client. No assessment of weight, no assessment of credibility, misrepresenting or overlooking the reality that the witness hadn't testified but was a paper witness in every sense of the word. None of that is considered in the Prosecution response yesterday. But, Your Honours, I have to move on. The rest of those answers are in our questions -- in our written skeleton. Your Honour, the evidence anyway is that belligerents defending the village are either 30 metres away from the location and a hundred metres away. So the Prosecution can't say that there was intentional targeting, we say. Given the foundational finding that shells are indiscriminate, we say, it falls to be reversed. Your Honour, I'll go to P1351. And again, on that last issue, no evidence at all from the Judges or from the -- that the -- HVO knew that civilians were in the basement as opposed to lawful belligerents. 1351. Now, Your Honour, the Prosecution say that Mr. Stojic was aware of the nature of this document, and we have asserted throughout that it wasn't received by him. No stamp on the document. No evidence it's received. And I would ask you to consider in due course, even on the face of it, how it compares with P03418 and 3D03065, both of those documents. One is addressed to Bruno Stojic as opposed to the Department of Defence, and the other one specifies for the attention of Bruno Stojic. But, Your Honours, even assuming that document is received by Stojic, it doesn't establish that the killings mentioned were foreseeable. It doesn't say that they were murder or that they were unlawful, as opposed to incidental and collateral. So we say the Judges really were at a stretch and in fact fell into error by referring to that document to somehow bolster or to find intent on the part of Bruno Stojic. Your Honour, when one is considering this, I think the fundamental malady is that the majority seemed to approach the facts as if there's only one protagonist in the area - and that's the HVO - and that the arena is empty apart from the HVO and civilians, that it's a blank canvas upon which they can -- HVO can draw their own agendas. And the reality is far from it. There's action and reaction as true in reality in the law of physics as it was at the time in that part of the world. And the truth is made clear by the Prosecution in other cases, and we can put on the screen the Hadzihasanovic case. It's public record, it's the indictment in the Hadzihasanovic, in which the Judges -- in which the Prosecution contended and accepted that the ABiH was engaging in massive attack in June 1993. Look at the Tihomir Misic barracks. Mr. Karnavas spoke about it yesterday. It was after that incident when the Muslim members of the HVO attacked the Croatian members of the HVO. It was after that date that the majority found that there were widespread detentions of Muslim men. It was after that date that the majority found a system of deportations was introduced. It was from June, from that month, where the majority found that the JCE was expanded. And, Your Honour, rather than try to fit that complex arrangement of facts back to 1993, we say a reasonable Trial Chamber would have considered other alternative explanations; namely, action and reaction, cause and effect. And by failing to consider this other reasonable option available to a reasonable Trial Chamber, we say the majority fell into error. Your Honour, in relation to Grounds 25 and 26 and the mens rea, it's revealing that the Judges really haven't addressed the intention of Bruno Stojic in the Judgement. They say at paragraph 428 that Stojic intended to expel the Muslim population. That was the shared intention filing. But in relation to the 20 other crimes, 21 other crimes, no mention of intention, no express finding that he intended to participate in a JCE, no express finding that he had the required knowledge, no evidence, no mention of the fact that in a JCE an accused must intend to commit the underlying crimes. And there's a manifest range of crimes, from destruction of property to murder and everything in between. And one may intend one particular crime and not another crime. One may intend to destroy property but not intend to kill. No findings on that whatsoever. And if the Prosecution say, Well, it's not necessary, one can hark everything back to the original assertion that there's an intention to expel the Muslim population, we say that's incorrect. Because even if one takes the domination for ethnic cleansing, it doesn't automatically, legally mean the same thing, that because you intend ethnic cleansing, you intend murder. So this is a legal judgement. Each finding has legal significance. And yet, one is sorry to say, that those type of typical findings have not been made by the majority. Your Honour, in relation to question 8, I would refer you again to the questions -- to the answers that are in the -- that have been handed up, we say it's important -- it's very clear both in relation to question 2 and Mostar that the Judges fell into error again in relation to IHL and the laws and customs of war, in relation to when they found that the Mostar bridge had a clear military utility and indeed was essential. They couldn't then find on the facts of this case that somehow its destruction amounted to a breach of those fundamental principles. And to somehow say, Well, one can be compliant -- IHL-compliant in relation to terms of distinction and targeting but still be responsible under persecution, for example, that has massive policy indications that we say are not supported by the law or practice. In relation to 8, question 8, Your Honour, I won't say more than what's in our written answers. Your Honour, the only argument or the only case I'm aware of at least that the Prosecution could refer to to somehow defend the majority decision - because, of course, they have the advantage on being on very solid territory, they're defending clean sweep of convictions and very hefty sentences - and they may say, No, the Judges are entitled to do that is reasonable. Well, the first observation, the test is not whether or not a particular decision is reasonable. That's not the test. The test is whether it's the only option open, the only reasonable option open beyond reasonable doubt, not just whether or not a particular finding is reasonable. But if one looks at Djordjevic, the Prosecution seek to cite that case to you which is somewhat similar, that there wasn't an express finding as to the intent in relation to underlying crime, we would seek to distinguish it for a number of reasons. Firstly, that case the Trial Chamber talked about requisite intent, which has a difference anyway from the intent to ethnically cleanse found by the majority. But that was a one-hander, there was one accused in that case, and a narrow group of crimes that was alleged. Here we have six accused and a very wide-ranging crimes, 21 different crimes, that are alleged in the case. And that Djordjevic case, even then, Your Honours, as the Appeals Chamber said it would be preferable to clearly state -- make a finding of intent in relation to each crime. Here it wasn't preferable; we say it was absolutely essential. The majority repeatedly deal with the group as a monolithic structure. I mentioned earlier the one mention of Mr. Bruno Stojic. I talked about the mention of how they described this undefined group, the HZ(R)HB. But, Your Honours, some of the accused may have intended all of the crimes; some, none of the crimes; some may have intended one of the crimes. Your Honours can't conduct a proper appellate review given the scarcity of the findings by the majority. And their failure to make proper findings effectively means that they failed to consider, properly consider individual criminal responsibility at all. Your Honours, I will skip quite a lot. In relation to Ground 15 again we would rest on the arguments in our brief, but if I can just talk about the Mladic diaries. Because it was really the Mladic diaries that was the foundations of the majority finding that Mr. Stojic was linked as an individual to the JCE, uncorroborated hearsay. Defence had no opportunity to confront the sole evidence to support that finding. We deal with that argument on Ground 16, but we say it is not a conjured-up argument; there's real meat to it. In circumstances where the Prosecution are allowed to introduce that type of evidence 18 months after they close the case, to deny the Defence the right to confront that evidence is really a gross abuse of discretion, and it is fatal to the proper consideration of these Mladic diaries. Your Honours, there has not been -- in fact, it is so serious that it runs the risk of infecting this whole decision, because one can aim for the stars but in human rights terms we must make sure that Trial Chamber reach a minimum standard of due process. And by acting in that manner and refusing the Defence leave to appeal means that an important finding - upon which the guilt of Mr. Stojic was reached - has simply not been addressed. Your Honours, there's much more that I can say, but I have to give time to my learned friend, Ms. Nozica. If, fortuitously, she manages to be quicker than the time she needs, I have something more to say, but with your leave. Your Honour, in short, we simply say that looking at our grounds in detail, you do have an unenviable task. I apologise we have 52 grounds; it's a lot. The grounds have substance. They deserve proper consideration. It is a gargantuan task. But justice is not easy. We say that Mr. Stojic, looking at the indictment itself as the vehicle for proving his culpability, has been occasioned a miscarriage of justice by the majority. And we say their numerous errors of law are so pervasive and so numerous that litter the entire judgement, reversible is appropriate in this case. Your Honour, with no further ado, I'll pass the floor, with your leave, to lead counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Thank you, Mr. Kahn.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My learned friend wanted to perhaps add something after I have finished, but I'm afraid even I will not have enough time to share with you everything we have prepared. We have raced against time throughout the trial, and we always had difficulty fitting everything we wanted to do within the time allocated; in particular, because this is a very voluminous case, with many, many documents and arguments to present before the Chamber. My learned friend discussed some of the irregularities applied by the majority when they approached the documents and evidence as well as the facts in this case. I just wanted to briefly turn to the errors made by the majority as regards the JCE and the doctrine itself. I will be very brief. There two categories. I deal with more with theory and I will try to do my best not to overlap with what my colleague has said. I will discuss the theoretical aspect, a very specific dimension of the JCE as found by the majority. There are two categories of errors when it came to the application of the JCE standard by the majority. I will first briefly summarise our arguments. First of all, the Trial Chamber misapplied the JCE as a criterion to defy common criminal purpose by concluding that they share the common political and military goal as sufficient to satisfy the element, although in and of themselves they are not criminal. This error is present in every aspect of the Trial Chamber's decision and calls for reversal because the JCE described by the Trial Chamber, which was allegedly spear-headed by Franjo Tudjman, Gojko Susak, and Janko Bobetko, could not have existed. Indeed the only common purpose that the Trial Chamber asserted that these individuals shared was the political purpose of a united Croat nation, and that political purpose is the only common factor in what the Trial Chamber described as a single JCE. If that JCE did not exist, then the liability of Mr. Stojic would be eviscerated, not only under JCE 1 but also under JCE form 3, which is predicated on the existence of JCE 1. Secondly, the Trial Chamber misapplied the JCE form 3 standard for identifying the outer reach of criminal acts attributable to a JCE member by allowing virtually any act to be deemed foreseeable in the context of a war, without making a finding that each act was made in furtherance of the alleged JCE 1 crimes. A standard of what is foreseeable in war is as unlimited as the possibilities for violence and does not provide a manageable standard. In assessing the Trial Chamber's decision on these issues, the Appellate Chamber reviews the findings of law to determine whether or not they are correct, that is Brdjanin appeals judgement, paragraph 10; and whether an error has a chance of changing the outcome of the decision, Brdjanin appeals judgement paragraph 9. As I will explain shortly, the Trial Chamber was incorrect in applying the JCE standard and reversal is certain to change the outcome of the decision. As already referenced, I will address two specific categories of error in the application of JCE doctrine, but I think it is useful to recall at the outset that the joint criminal enterprise doctrine has been, beginning with the Tadic case, a controversial doctrine that has drawn criticism, as my learned friend Mr. Kahn mentioned. Indeed, at the time the Tribunal was established by the United Nations Security Council, it was clear that it was not supposed to create new law. Thus, at the time the Council voted, the representative of the People's Republic of China, Ambassador Li Zhaoxing explained that China's vote in favour of the resolution was a political position that should not be construed as an endorsement of the legal approach involved. China, he said, believed that an international tribunal should be established by concluding a treaty so as to provide a solid legal foundation for it and ensure its effective functioning, and that the Chinese delegation emphasises that the international Tribunal established in the current matter can only be an ad hoc arrangement suited only to the special circumstances of the former Yugoslavia and shall not constitute any precedent. Similarly, Ambassador Sir David Hannay of the United Kingdom stated: The Statute does not, of course, create new law but reflects existing international law in this field. There's no need to reconsider the characteristics of the doctrine of the JCE, but we believe that it needs to be strictly limited to the elements enunciated in prior case law, which all must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. In insisting on this, we are only asking this Chamber to restate what it already held in the Brdjanin decision, which was careful to delineate a clear set of limiting principles. The decision warned that untethered from its core elements, JCE becomes an open-ended concept that permits convictions based on guilt by association. Brdjanin appeals judgement, paragraph 428. The Brdjanin decision also addressed and squarely rejected a proposal by the Prosecution team that JCE doctrine should be tailored as a matter of policy to allow the Tribunal to prosecute and punish those who participate in international crimes as leaders, and not only as subordinates. Brdjanin appeals judgement paragraph 421. As the Brdjanin decision correctly held, such policy considerations are inapposite as a basis for a theory of individual criminal responsibility. Accordingly, Brdjanin restated the elements of JCE and re-emphasised that each element must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt as to each participant, lest the doctrine be reduced to absurdity. It is paragraph 428 I've already referred to. First, the accused must possess the requisite criminal intent which can be found only if this is the only reasonable inference on the evidence. Second, the trier of fact must find that the intent was shared by a plurality of persons as a common criminal purpose. Third, it must be shown beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused made a contribution to the criminal purpose. And finally it must be shown that the intended crime actually took place. Brdjanin appeals judgement paragraph 430. The Trial Chamber purported to make all these findings, but it actually revised doctrine dramatically, effectuating in the process a miscarriage of justice and wreaking havoc on international criminal law. In short, Mr. Stojic was convicted under, first, a theory of guilt by association; and second, a theory that he - as alleged head of the Defence Department of the HVO HZ HB - assumed responsibility for all acts carried out by its armed forces and in its name. This occurred in three principal ways. First, the Trial Chamber found a JCE based on an alleged geopolitical goal purportedly shared by Republic of Croatia and HVO leaders of expanding Croatia's borders to create a united Croat nation, which is not, in and of itself, a crime. The Defence does not in any way accept that such geopolitical goal existed at any time, which has been well documented through the Republic of Croatia and the HVO unquestionable commitment to any of the peace proposals presented by the international community. None of such proposals included expanding of Croatia's borders. The Trial Chamber, however, criminalised a political objective rather than finding a common criminal purpose, and then identified a set of individuals who shared that political purpose as the core of the JCE. Although the HVO was, certainly, not a political party but a spontaneously formed self-defence organisation, it could be asserted that this holding has devastating implications for political parties and movements around the world, and I mean primarily such political movements aiming at liberating particular territories whose ultimate goal may be to change borders. Second, the judgement proposes that participation in a JCE can occur through a combination of routine military orders which the HVO with its structure in forming could not issue any way alleged authority to conduct military operations and alleged inaction. This finding again substitutes proof of a legitimate, if disfavoured, goal - being military action or even aggression - for proof beyond reasonable doubt of illegitimate means that are criminalised by the Statute; and it substitutes the requirement that the accused make an affirmative contribution to the action with a finding of purported inaction. The ultimate effect is to turn what some might view in hindsight as ineffective leadership or military missteps into a war crime. Third, the Trial Chamber's decision erred further in applying an open-ended concept of JCE 3 to exacerbate the misidentified JCE 1 purposes and to effectively render all members of a political or military leadership criminally liable for the offences of their armed forces, regardless of whether there was a causal nexus or - to put it another way - foreseeability between those crimes and the alleged JCE 1 crimes that constitute the individuals' alleged contribution to the JCE. The Appeals Chamber is certainly aware of the positions held by Stojic during the relevant period and his defences stand thereon. Nevertheless, it could be said that the Trial Chamber's view places political and military leaders, especially those in dire circumstances such as were present in the crumbling former Yugoslavia, in the impossible position of either abandoning their lawful political objectives midstream and thereby betraying those vulnerable people who are the intended beneficiaries of those efforts; or risk war crimes prosecution for all acts of anyone who can, in hindsight, be associated with them. None of this can supported by any Tribunal precedent on JCE doctrine or the Statute governing the Tribunal, and has no precedent in international law. The Trial Chamber found a JCE by a plurality of persons, including, inter alia, Franjo Tudjman, Gojko Susak, and Janko Bobetko, and further on Bruno Stojic. It is the judgement, volume 4, paragraph 1231. Under established precedent, the Trial Chamber was required to identify a common criminal purpose to the JCE and to find that each participant shared that purpose. Brdjanin appeals judgement, paragraphs 429 and 430 as discussed by my learned friend Mr. Kahn. But even accepting the Trial Chamber's flawed view of the facts, the only purported purpose identified by the Trial Chamber that these individuals each harboured and shared was to set up a Croatian entity that reconstituted, at least in part, the borders of the Banovina of 1939 and facilitate the reunification of the Croatian people. Judgement, volume 4, paragraph 24. Even -- even, I emphasise - if that were a goal shared by these individuals - and the evidence shows that the reality was far more complex - a JCE must involve the commission of a crime provided for in the Statute of the ICTY, as stated in the Gotovina trial judgement, paragraph 1953, and the Statute does not criminalise any political goal. In trying to link the alleged participants to the goal of reconstituting the Banovina rather than to the goal of murder, deportation, genocide, et cetera, the Trial Chambers adopted an unheard of JCE doctrine, that people who join in or espouse any common goal or at least any war time goal, incur the risk of criminal liability if some members who share that goal commit war crimes. That was a profound error as well as an absurd one. The Martic appeals judgement reaffirms that political intentions are not sufficient to establish a joint criminal purpose. Martic appeals judgement, paragraphs 123 and 124. This principle follows from the Tadic case itself, which holds that a JCE requires a common criminal purpose, not merely a common purpose, for engaging in a war or politics. Other judgements of this Tribunal are no different in that respect following Tadic. I just wanted to remind you of the Stakic judgement and the appeals judgement in Brdjanin. I believe the standards of the JCE were applied correctly in light of this appeal, in particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am aware of the time and I am also aware of the fact that if something is missing from the transcript, I spoke in vain; but I will nevertheless try to slow down. All of these cases demonstrate, consistent with the language of the ICTY Statute, that a desire to control a territory, even by military means, is not per se sufficient to establish the existence of a JCE. And therefore, a finding that individuals shared the goal of creating a new Banovina does not inherently involve or suggest any criminal intent. The Trial Chamber did not find that all the alleged members of the JCE shared a criminal purpose. To be sure, the Trial Chamber identified a single common criminal purpose of domination by the HZ(R)HB Croats through ethnic cleansing of the Muslim population. Judgement, volume 4, paragraph 41. But it failed to find that the members of the JCE shared that purpose. That is exemplified most obviously by the Trial Chamber's condemnation of Tudjman, Susak, and Bobetko, who could only be tied to the JCE insofar as they shared the ultimate goal of a united Croatian people. And if these three individuals were not JCE members, then there was no JCE. Applying the established standards referred to above, the Stojic's Defence argument is that there was no other JCE with or without aforesaid individuals. Indeed, these individuals were expressly identified as participants in the JCE, and their alleged views about a united Croat nation were evaluated at length. Judgement, volume 4, paragraphs 4 to 24 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 6 to 24.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But they were never found to have harboured an intent to commit a crime committed by the Statute. The closest the Trial Chambers came to such a finding is at volume 4, paragraph 43, which states that: "As of December 1991, certain leaders of Croatia, including Franjo Tudjman, believed that to achieve the political purpose" of a reunited Croatian people "it was necessary to change the ethnic makeup of territories claimed to form part of the HZ(R)HB." Judgement, volume 4, paragraph 43. But this finding is vague and equivocal, alleging a belief that it was necessary to change the ethnic makeup of territories without discussing what this meant, whether it represented any plan of action, but what mean it would be accomplished, or - most fundamentally -- why it was necessary. It thus falls well short of a finding beyond a reasonable doubt of an intent to carry out a criminal purpose. The equivocation in this finding is a result of an absence of evidence to support an actual finding of criminal intent. Exhibit P00089 the Trial Chamber cited says nothing about forceable removable of civilians from their homes, but records another individual - not Tudjman - discussing boundaries and aspirations of a Croat state. There is no criminal activity discussed or criminal intent referenced. Moreover, the Trial Chamber admitted in the very next paragraph, judgement, volume 4, paragraph 44, that the evidence does not support a finding that there was an agreement concerning a common criminal design prior to mid-January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] So within the context of identifying the common criminal purpose sufficient for a JCE, this finding refutes any notion that a common criminal purpose had been achieved prior to January 1993, so evidence from December 1991 cannot be sufficient to show a JCE. The other reference cited to support a finding of Tudjman's intent to participate in a JCE is at paragraph 522 of volume 4 of the Trial Chamber's Judgement, which also occurred prior to the JCE time period, which is to say 11 September 1992. And although Mr. Tudjman is selectively quoted as calling for Croatia to be cleansed, this reference to Croatia is to the Republic of Croatia, not majority-Croat proportions of Bosnia, as the underlying Exhibit P466 makes clear; whereas cleansing meant repelling Serbian forces from inside Croatia, which has nothing to do with cleansing any ethnic group from either Bosnia-Herzegovina or Croatia. Beyond these items, the only other references to these individuals from the correct time-frame are: One, a statement by President Izetbegovic to Tudjman warning against ethnic cleansing - and no indication that Tudjman disagreed. That's Judgement volume 4, paragraph 52. And, second, a letter from an international organisation copying Tudjman and stating that the organisation would not help Croat peoples move from Serbian-controlled territory of HVO and again no indication of Tudjman's view or response, much less action. Judgement volume 4, paragraph 54. Tudjman's silence does not prove that he, let alone Susak or Bobetko, intended to effectuate a common criminal purpose - Tadic appeals judgement, paragraph 195 - or made any contribution to such a purpose. All of this amounts to far less than the showing of criminal purpose in the Gotovina Appeals Chamber decision which rejected a finding of a JCE based on ambiguous transcripts, lawful efforts to help civilians temporarily depart from a war zone, and a series of political speeches by Franjo Tudjman. That's Gotovina, paragraphs 89 to 98. The gravamen of the offence of the supposed participants in the JCE, then, was not ordering, planning or inciting crimes, but for the sake of argument, in allegedly adopting a view about where the borders of a nation emerging from a failed state should fall. This is simply insufficient to establish a JCE. Moreover, as noted above, neither the Republic of Croatia nor the HVO ever undertook any activities which could be deemed as a redrawing of internationally recognised borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The evidence presented during the trial proved just the contrary. Briefly, therefore, the Trial Chamber's legal findings in this regard are not an anomaly nor are they trivial. In a nutshell, the Trial Chamber's factual findings at best amount to, one, a relatively inchoate dream or goal by Tudjman and other Croat leaders for a united Croat nation that included territory within Bosnia-Herzegovina; and, two, the alleged efforts by some alleged members of the common enterprise in support of that goal, including by military intervention in Bosnia-Herzegovina; and, three, the acts of some HVO soldiers that amounted to war crimes. That is pure guilt by association. The fact that some HVO members and units committed criminal acts does not establish a common criminal purpose for the entire HVO and this theory was repudiated as the basis for the JCE in Brdjanin. The Trial Chamber erred in not considering the extent in which the HVO's -- were legitimate, that is, not criminal. The Trial Chamber therefore applied the wrong standard, and the standard it applied has grave implications for political parties and movements which frequently must contend with extremist elements in their own ranks. Indeed, the Trial Chamber's holding in places the burden on all the other members and leadership to abandon the party of movement immediately [as interpreted]. Everything said so far demonstrates that the Trial Chamber's findings on Stojic and the other accused cannot be affirmed, but that is only the first of the Trial Chamber's many legal errors. Its second error is of the same ilk. It found the JCE based on alleged intent to engage in military action, the alleged authority to take or prevent war crimes that occurred as part of the actions of others, and the alleged inaction upon knowledge of ongoing war crimes. But even more fundamentally, the Chamber may and should resolve the issue squarely on the law because a legitimate application of JCE doctrine should not permit Mr. Stojic's conviction on this basis. The HVO was primarily a Defence force which neither showed any intention to commence military conflict, nor it could be blamed for outbreak of such conflict. Therefore, the following doctrine could not be applied thereto. Nevertheless, the Stojic Defence points to the JCE doctrine which should not allow criminalisation of the intent to engage in military action for the same reason it does not criminalise the intent to achieve a geopolitical goal. The Statute of the ICTY does not cover such an action which is not listed in sections 2, 3, 4, or 5. Moreover, it is critical to understand that Mr. Stojic was a civilian with no military role. He was not a member of the armed forces. As to the purpose of promoting reconciliation and healing, the dissenting Judge below aptly asked: How will we achieve reconciliation if we place everyone in the same boat? In a situation that devolved into warfare and ethnic cleansing as tragically as the situation did in the former Yugoslavia, it a matter of simple logic that some people acted dishonourably. Some failed to exhibit exemplary, courageous, and virtuous behaviour, and these will have much to answer for in their consciences. Indeed, some of these may be liable under the civil or criminal law in the courts of the nations with jurisdiction over the relevant territory. But theories of liability that can draw into an international criminal Tribunal anyone who potentially could have done more to stop the violence and bloodshed risks being brought without limit. This in turn means that the individuals actually held responsibile can be viewed as political victims rather than perpetrators of war crimes and the Tribunal itself as existing to make a political point rather than to serve the ends of blind justice. That was the notion rejected in Brdjanin and it should be rejected again here. Thus the Appeals Chamber should reject the Trial Chambers Court's -- the Trial Court's JCE 1 analysis and overturn Mr. Stojic's conviction on this basis. Thank you, Your Honours.
