utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Barbara Goy and I will responding today to Your Honours' question number 1 and Grounds 54 and 55 of Stojic's appeal relating to the international nature of the armed conflict and the state of occupation. And Mr. Menon will afterwards respond to the grounds of appeal relating to JCE responsibility and answer questions 4(c) and 8. But before we begin our response, I would just like to briefly address a procedural matter in relation to the Defence written answers to Your Honours' questions. Your Honours, these written submissions were presented by the Defence as skeleton arguments. This implied that the Defence would be covering them in their oral argument and it is our understanding that Your Honours ruled on this basis, that there would be an aid to follow the oral submissions. This was not the instruction in Your Honours' preparation order which sought oral answers to the questions and no additional briefings. This puts, of course, the Prosecution at a disadvantage having to respond in a two-hour slot not only to the submissions on the grounds but also answer the questions. We would therefore ask Your Honours to disregard the written submission inasmuch as they are not covered during the oral argument.

utterances.text: Madam, they are not going to be considered as part of the records, full stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: On that note, we will then start with responding orally to Your Honours' question 1. Your Honours have asked whether as a legal matter the Trial Chamber erred in inquiring into the existence of a state of occupation on the basis that there was no armed conflict in some places and on some dates or whether such inquiry was necessary on the basis that people in and property on occupied territory are afforded additional or other protection under the Geneva Conventions. The short answer is that this inquiry was only necessary for Count 19, the grave breach of extensive destruction of property under Article 2. Let me take Your Honours through the reasons for this response. For grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions under Article 2 of the Statute, two levels need to be distinguished: The general applicability of the Geneva Conventions and the protection of persons and property under the Geneva Conventions depending on the specific breach in question. For the general applicability of Article 2 of the ICTY Statute, it was not necessary to inquire whether a state of occupation existed. According to Common Article 2 of the Geneva Conventions, the Geneva Conventions apply when there is an international armed conflict or a state of occupation. Once an armed conflict of an international nature is established, international humanitarian law applies throughout the territories of the parties to the conflict. The Appeals Chamber held this already in the 1995 Tadic Appeals Chamber decision on jurisdiction, in paragraphs 68 and 70, and confirmed it in the Kordic Appeal Judgement in paragraph 319. The Appeals Chamber in Kordic said: "The Tadic appeal decision on jurisdiction explains that the very nature of the Geneva Conventions, particularly, Geneva Conventions 3 and 4, dictates the application throughout the territories of the parties to the conflict. Any other construction would substantially defeat their purpose." The Trial Chamber in this case, however, disregarded this law when it made piecemeal findings on the existence of the armed conflict for the purpose of establishing whether Article 2 of the Statute applies. While as a matter of law this approach is incorrect, the Prosecution has not appealed it because it did not impact the verdict. The Chamber stated that it received a substantial amount of evidence pertaining to the existence of an armed conflict throughout BiH. That's volume 3, paragraph 514. And it also determined that the conflict was international in nature; volume 3, paragraph 568. But then it concluded that an armed conflict existed, in particular municipalities at particular points in time, such as in Prozor municipality in October 1992 and in April and July 1993. That's volume 3, paragraph 514. Based on this piecemeal approach it then found it necessary to inquire into the state of occupation rather than reaching the conclusions that the Geneva Conventions III and IV applied throughout the territories of the parties to the conflict. It is this erroneous understanding that led the Chamber to hold in volume 1, paragraph 575 -- volume 3, excuse me, paragraph 575: "It is, however, necessary to establish the existence of an occupation when crimes are alleged under Article 2 of the Statute in places and dates for which the Chamber has been unable to establish the existence of a conflict between the ABiH and the HVO." This brings me to the second half of the question, whether the Chamber was required to look into the question of occupation to determine the protection of persons or property for the purpose of the specific grave breach in question.For the grave breaches regime under Article 2 of the Statute to apply, the persons and property must be protected by the Geneva Conventions. And here we need to distinguish between the crimes against persons and the crimes against property. In relation to persons, Article 4 of Geneva Convention IV defines protected persons as those who are either in the hands of a party to the conflict of which they are not nationals or in occupied territory. Thus, persons are not only protected in occupied territory, but also when they are in the hands of a party to the conflict of which they are not nationals. And nationality, as we know since Tadic, can be understood as allegiance. As the Trial Chamber recognised in volume 1, paragraph 101, with reference to the ICRC commentary to the Geneva Conventions, the expression "in the hands of" has a very broad meaning and is limited to being directly in enemy hands as a prisoner. The ICRC commentary states: "It simply means that the person is in territory which is under the control of the power in question." That's page 47. Thus for the grave breaches regimes against persons, the Chamber did not have to inquire into the question of occupation. As regards the protection of property, the Chamber distinguished in paragraph 106 of volume 1 between property that is generally protected under the Geneva Conventions regardless of location, such as civilian hospitals, and property that only enjoys the protection when it is located in occupied territory. However, in relation to property that does not enjoy general protection, Geneva Conventions IV distinguishes between protection against appropriation and protection against destruction. Protection against appropriation does not depend on the property being located in occupied territory. This protection is listed in Article 33 of Geneva Convention IV which says: "Pillage is prohibited." And this Article 33 is in the section applicable to territories of a party to the conflict and to occupied territory. The Chamber acknowledged this in volume 1, paragraph 129, where it said: "This prohibition applies equally, moreover, to the territory of the parties to the conflict and to occupied territories." Protection against destruction, on the other hand, applies only in occupied territory. The protection is listed in Article 53 of Geneva Convention IV which is in the section dealing with occupied territory. This means only for the extensive destruction of property not justified by military necessity and carried out unlawfully and wantonly, Count 19, the Chamber was required to determine whether property which did not enjoy general protection was located in occupied territory. But even here, if no state of occupation was found, the same crime base would be covered by Count 19, wanton destruction as a war crime, under Article 3 -- covered by Count 20, excuse me, I misspoke, wanton destruction under Article 3. Your Honours, there is a third level to the analysis and I'm going to touch upon that briefly. I'm only mentioning this third level for sake of completeness on the question of the law because it doesn't arise on the facts of this case. This third level relates to the details of the protection of persons and property. For displacement crimes, the border of occupied territory amounts to a border for deportation as the Chamber recognised in volume 3, paragraph 575. Occupation can also be relevant because certain conduct may be specifically permitted in occupied territory. For example, in relation to appropriation of property, Article 55 of Geneva Convention IV contains specific rules for occupied territory authorising the occupying powers under certain conditions to requisition of private property, such as food and medical supplies, to meet the needs of the occupying forces of the administration. The Chamber recognised this as well in volume 1, paragraph 130. But on the facts of this case, this third level did not require a finding of occupation because when we look through the Chamber's findings on deportation, they did not hinge on the notion of occupied territory and none of the special circumstances permitting certain conduct in occupied territory were made out. Unless Your Honours have any questions in relation to our answer on question 1, I would then turn to Ground 54 of Stojic's appeal in relation to the international nature of the armed conflict. The international nature of the armed conflict not only matters because a number of crimes were charged under Article 2 of the Statute. The international nature of the armed conflict also matters because it accurately reflects what happened in this case: The role Croatia played in the events which form the basis for this case. The Trial Chamber's conclusion that the conflict between the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna, the HVO, and the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the ABiH, was international in nature is reasonable and consistent with the Tribunal's conclusions in other cases such as Blaskic, Kordic, and Naletilic and Martinovic. The Chamber reasonably found that the conflict was international on two grounds: Direct intervention of Croatia's armed forces in the armed conflict and Croatia's overall control over the HVO. Each of these grounds alone is sufficient to render the conflict international. I will address both in turn and start with Croatia's direct intervention. The Chamber reasonably concluded that Croatia, through its own forces, directly intervened in the conflict between the HVO and the ABiH. The evidence shows that Croatia's armed forces were not only present at the relevant times in the relevant locations as the Defence suggests but were also directly participating in the armed conflict. The fact that Croatia’s leadership attempted to hide this further confirms Croatia's direct involvement. The Chamber reviewed the evidence in the locations and at the times where it had found an armed conflict existed according to its piecemeal approach, and it reasonably concluded that Croatia's armed forces were directly involved in the conflict against the ABiH at the relevant times. This covers the entire period from the attack in Prozor in October 1992 to the armed conflict in Mostar in early 1994. The evidence relied upon by the Chamber as well as other evidence on the record show that Croatia's armed forces were not only present but directly involved in the armed conflict against the ABiH. For example, the Chamber relied on numerous pieces of evidence to show that the attack on Prozor in October 1992 was carried out by a combination of HVO forces and Croatia's army such as Exhibit P1542, according to which very strong forces of HVO and Croatian army attacked the town with tanks and heavy artillery. An ECMM report of 3 June 1993 confirms that the Filipovic Brigade from Zagreb took part in the HVO offensives against Jablanica, an offensive which we know took place in April 1993 and led to a number of crimes which form part of the common plan. Exhibit P02627. In April 1993, ABiH commander Arif Pasalic complained to UNPROFOR and the EU that two different HV brigades were stationed in the region Capljina, Stolac, Dubrava and carried out combat activities directed at the ABiH; Exhibit P02043. And Capljina and Stolac fall within the indictment municipalities. On 15 July 1993, Petkovic, at the time chief of the HVO Main Staff, sent a report to the Defence Department of the HVO Main Staff which states under the heading "Our forces": "Out of 700 men from the battalion of the HV 5th Guards Motorised Brigade, 400 men are for attack. During the attack on 10 July 1993 in the area of -- south of Mostar Gnjojnice, its task was to cut off the Muslim forces and take Gnjojnice." Exhibit P03466. So the HV, the Army of Croatia, carried out an offensive operation against the ABiH in territories claimed by the JCE members. Later, in October 1993, Croatia's army 5th Guards Brigade reported to the Croatian Ministry of Defence that an order issued by the chief of the Croatian army Main Staff, the 3rd Motorised Battalion has been transferred to Ploce and upon its arrival it has been deployed in offensive operations in the area of Mostar battle-field. The battalion numbered 367 men. Exhibit P06037. In January 1994, the commander of the 1st Company of the 3rd Military Police Battalion of the HVO in Buna, in Mostar municipality, sent the following report to the Herceg-Bosna Ministry of Defence: "Immediately after receipt of this order," and then follows a description of the order, "we established contact with the command of the Croatian army located in our zone of responsibility." Exhibit P07742. This shows there was a command of the Croatian army in Mostar municipality, an area which falls within the common plan. And the report further states: "We encountered full understanding on their part and they helped us a lot by ordering their soldiers to remove all insignia, proving their membership in the Croatian army." Your Honours, this evidence shows that the Croatia army units were not only present but involved in the armed conflict against the ABiH. That there might not have been evidence in relation to direct involvement in all relevant municipalities does not affect the reasonableness of the Chamber's conclusion. The conclusion remains reasonable because the character of the conflict is determined overall, as the Chamber correctly pointed out in volume 3, paragraph 518. Turning to my second point. The evidence also confirms that Croatia's leadership was trying to hide the direct involvement of Croatia's army in this conflict. The evidence shows that insignia of Croatian army were removed - we have seen this in the exhibit I have just mentioned - and that the label of "volunteers" was used to hide the involvement. Let me say a few words about the use of "volunteers." Croatian army forces were present in Bosnia on order of Croatia. In particular, the presence and involvement of units cannot be explained, as the Defence tries to argue, by individuals who volunteered their services to the HVO. In fact, Praljak in his reply in paragraph 7 points out that the units could not go out of Croatia without supreme commander's order. And as we've seen from the exhibits I mentioned in the beginning of my submissions, units of Croatia's army were participating in the armed conflict. Croatian armed forces were in BiH on order of Croatia regardless of whether they could volunteer to serve in BiH rather than in Croatia. Even if their presence was voluntary in BiH in the sense that they volunteered to serve in BiH rather than in Croatia, once they so volunteered, they were then deployed by Croatia, they were involved in the armed conflict on order of Croatia. That these so-called volunteers were sent by Croatia is confirmed by Croatian President Tudjman himself. And I'm referring to a conversation between Tudjman and, among others, Croatia's Minister of Defence Gojko Susak and the HVO Main Staff General Janko Bobetko on 6 November 1993, where we see Tudjman planning military operations in province 10 of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Tudjman says: "Kiseljak has become important to us so that we can link up with Busovaca. Now at this moment it is necessary also that we should try to link up Kiseljak, Kresevo with Busovaca, Novi Travnik, that is, with the entire territory here, at once take control of Gornji Vakuf for the purpose of linkage with Novi Travnik ..." And then he continues: "We have to do all this, of course, under the cover of sending volunteers." That's Exhibit P06485, page 2, the presidential transcript of 6 November 1993. The cover of volunteers is also evident from another conversation between Tudjman, Susak, and Bobetko a few weeks later, on 23 November 1993. Here we see Tudjman outraged at the exposure of Croatia's direct involvement in the armed conflict between the HVO and the ABiH. Tudjman says: "Thirdly, how, Minister of Defence and chief of the main headquarters, could you have issued an order confirming that Croatia is waging war, that it is directly involved, and I constantly emphasise ... you should have build this up as something voluntary, that these are volunteers who have left the Croatian army, who fight there under HVO command, and here you are appointing the main headquarters." That's Exhibit P06839, page 8. I repeat the exhibit number, Exhibit P06839, page 8 -- Exhibit P06831, page 8, apologies. The presidential transcript of 23 November 1993. This shows Tudjman's anger at how his subordinates could have created a document which so plainly shows Croatia's directly involvement when this should have been done under the cover of volunteers. That these were not real volunteers also explains why Croatia paid the salary of Croatian army personnel deployed in BiH as the Chamber found in volume 3, paragraph 529. Croatia would not be paying real volunteers that cut theirs ties with the Croatian army and volunteered their service in the HVO. Your Honours, by using the label of "volunteers," Croatia's leadership thus tried to hide Croatia's direct intervention, an intervention which is amply supported by the evidence. On the basis of the totality of the evidence, the Chamber's finding that Croatia directly intervened with its armed forces in the conflict between the HVO and the ABiH is reasonable. Let me now turn to the second factor, overall control. The Chamber also reasonably found that the conflict was international because of Croatia's overall control over the HVO as an organised, hierarchically structured group. The Chamber relied on numerous manifestations of that control in -- but perhaps the clearest indication of Croatia's overall control is its involvement in organising, coordinating, and planning military operations against the ABiH. And I will limit my submissions today to this factor. The evidence shows that Croatian President Tudjman organised and planned military actions in BiH against the ABiH. And I will limit myself to the discussion of three meetings in November 1993. On 5 November 1993, in a meeting between Tudjman and representatives of Herceg-Bosna, in which Prlic, Praljak and Herceg-Bosna's president Mate Boban were present, Tudjman said: "We must organise ourselves so as to defend the line we have managed to conquer and have received permission to keep at the international conference, i.e., the line between Novi Travnik, Vitez and Busovaca." And after having received information about the situation around Vares, Tudjman gave the following instruction: "Transfer what remains of the troops from Vares to Kiseljak and push through to Busovaca." That's Exhibit P06454, pages 20 and 62, the presidential transcript of 5 November 1993. And what these actions are aimed at becomes clear when Tudjman said: "The problem then boils down to our securing in the border [sic] sense the borders of the Republic Herceg-Bosna as favorably as we can." That's on page 80. So Tudjman expresses the view that it is Croatia that has to fight for Herceg-Bosna's borders. The next day, on 6 November 1993, in a meeting with, among others, Susak and Bobetko, we see Tudjman and General Bobetko planning military operations in Gornji Vakuf and Novi Travnik. Bobetko: "In the next eight days, we have to take Gornji Vakuf and in that way solve that -- better to say create completely different operational conditions for our further inroads, defensive and offensive." "Tudjman: We are in agreement here, General, please, what have you got ready in the way of manpower and material to give them so that they can do that?" And then follows an explanation by Bobetko which concludes with: "We will give forces, we will take out the front -- we will take out of the front the least reinforced ... say a thousand armed men and resort to the liquidation of Bugojno and then we'll go onwards. "Tudjman: Liquidate? "Bobetko: Take. "Tudjman: Gornji Vakuf, surely. "Bobetko: Yes, Gornji Vakuf, and blockade this." That's Exhibit P6485, pages 10 and 11, presidential transcript of 6 November 1993. On 10 November 1993, Tudjman confirms this instruction in relation to Gornji Vakuf in a meeting with Prlic and others, where he says: "You know that I sent a new commander and ordered that new volunteers be sent to defend the Vitez line, that is to say, Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, and to bring this Gornji Vakuf to an end, and later Bugojno." That's Exhibit P06581, page 18, the presidential transcript of 10 November 1993. This one sentence confirms that Tudjman gave instruction for military action, that Tudjman ordered so-called volunteers to be sent, and that Tudjman sent commanders to be involved in the conflict. Your Honours, although I've highlighted three presidential transcripts of November 1993, this overall control was present throughout the conflict. We can see this, for example, in the fact that from autumn 1992 to 24 July 1993 Praljak had de facto command authority over the HVO armed forces although he had no formal position then in the HVO but was Croatia's assistant minister of defence. Volume 4, paragraph 482. And Your Honours will hear more about it tomorrow during the Prosecution's response to Praljak's appeal. To conclude, Your Honours, the Chamber's conclusion that Croatia exercised overall control over the HVO is reasonable and Stojic's Ground 54 in relation to the international armed conflict should be dismissed. This brings me to the last part of my submission. Unless Your Honours have questions, that would be Ground 55 on occupation. The Chamber's conclusion that a state of occupation existed in eight municipalities for a certain period of time was reasonable. Croatia occupied these municipalities by proxy through its overall control over the HVO. The HVO in turn not only had the ability to control the territory but did, in fact, exercise its authority over the territory. It exercised its authority either because it had attacked the relevant areas with HVO armed forces before or because HVO armed forces carried out mass arrests of the Muslim population in the respective municipalities. The HVO issued orders to the local population, plundered and destroyed Muslim property. That the HVO was able to behave in this way unhindered shows that the legitimate local government was rendered incapable of functioning. In a case of occupation by proxy or agency, two different forms of control need to be distinguished: Croatia's control over the HVO and the HVO's control over the territory that is found to be occupied. And I will first address Croatia's control over the HVO before turning to the HVO's control over the territory. Croatia occupied the eight municipalities in BiH by proxy because forces on the ground, the HVO, can be considered organs of Croatia acting on behalf of Croatia in the sense that their acts can be attributed to Croatia. The Appeals Chamber in Tadic determined that control by a state over organised and hierarchically structured forces may be of an overall character. The Appeals Chamber made this finding for the purposes of determining the international nature of the conflict but the underlying reason similarly applies to occupation as it is a question of whether the acts of the forces can be attributed to a state or party to the armed conflict. The Chamber thus correctly relied on Croatia's overall control over the HVO as the applicable legal test, in volume 1, paragraph 96. And as I discussed before, the Chamber reasonably concluded that Croatia did exercise overall control over the HVO. As regards the HVO's control over the territory, the Chamber correctly focussed on the HVO's ability to exercise authority over the territory in line with customary international law set out in Article 42 of the annex to The Hague -- of the annex to the 1907 Hague Convention. Contrary to what the Defence suggests, the actual exercise of authority is not necessary. But Your Honours whether the ability to exercise authority is sufficient is not a question that arises on the facts of this case. The Chamber's findings and the evidence on the record show that the HVO did exercise authority over the territory and it did so in lieu of the local sovereign. I will address both aspects. The evidence shows that the HVO was not only able but actually did exercise its authority in the relevant locations at the relevant times. The HVO, through its military, exercised the authority by carrying out mass arrests, by issuing orders to the local population. For example, in Prozor, which the Chamber found occupied from August 1993 until December 1993, Muslim women, children, and elderly were kept at various locations in Prozor municipality and could not move about freely. Volume 2, paragraph 117. An ECMM report of 10 August 1993 states that most of the Muslim population is under house arrest. Exhibit P09619. Another example, in Stolac, which was occupied in July and August 1993, the HVO military and military police arrested women, children, and elderly and detained them first in a shop and then in a school building. Volume 3, paragraph 937. And the HVO exercised its authority by forcibly displacing the Muslim population. For example, the women, children, and elderly who were detained in the school were held there for three weeks and then transported to Buna in Mostar municipality and from there they had to walk to Blagaj. Volume 3, paragraph 937. Almost 1.200 Muslims were displaced from Stolac at that time. Volume 3, paragraph 939. Thus the Chamber's finding and the evidence show that the HVO did exercise authority over the relevant municipalities and it did so as a hostile force. Contrary to what the Defence suggests, the HVO was not the legitimate government and its armed forces, the HVO military, were a hostile army. In September 1992, the BiH Constitutional Court declared Herceg-Bosna unconstitutional. It annulled all its founding legislation, including Herceg-Bosna's decree on armed forces. That's volume 4, paragraph 426, citing Exhibit P -- volume 1, paragraph 426, citing Exhibit P00505. In any event, Your Honours, this is occupation by agency and there's no suggestion that Croatia had a sovereign title to the parts of BiH in question. That an armed conflict was going on at the same time does not undermine a finding of occupation either because there was no actual combat in the relevant areas which could undermine HVO's control over the territory. This is in line with one of the guide-lines set out in the Naletilic Trial Judgement on occupation in paragraph 217, guide-lines which the Trial Chamber in this case endorsed in paragraph 88. This guide-line says: "The enemy's forces have surrendered, been defeated, or withdrawn. In this respect, battle areas may not be considered as occupied territory. However, sporadic local resistance, even unsuccessful, does not affect the reality of occupation." That is Naletilic trial judgement paragraph 217 endorsed by the Prlic trial judgement in volume 1, paragraph 88. In each of the locations the -- that were found to be occupied, the ABiH was either defeated, had withdrawn or offered no resistance which was capable of undermining the HVO's control. That some of the occupation lasted only a short period of time, such as in Prozor from 24 to 30 October 1992, does not undermine the Chamber's conclusion either. There's no minimum time period for occupation. The Eritrea-Ethiopian Claims Commission, for example, accepted that a few days of military occupation could establish occupation. Your Honours will find that in our response to Stojic's appeal. That in some of the places the occupation did not follow an armed attack and invasion is similarly irrelevant. As set out in Article 2, paragraph 2 of Geneva Convention IV: "The Convention shall also apply to all cases of partial or total occupation of the territory of the high contracting party, even if the said occupation meets with no resistance." Turning lastly to the flip side of occupation, the incapacity of the legitimate local government to function. The legitimate BiH local government was incapable of functioning. This is inherent in the Chamber's findings that the HVO was able to freely destroy or steal Muslim property. The legitimate authority in BiH was the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina headed by Izetbegovic. Volume 1, paragraph 432 through 433. And, therefore, the legitimate local government was the Municipal Assembly recognised by that government and not any local HVO. As I mentioned before, in September 1993, the BiH Constitutional Court declared Herceg-Bosna unconstitutional and annulled all its founding legislation. Volume 1, paragraph 426. Therefore, the legitimate Bosnian authorities rejected Herceg-Bosna's authority and consequently also its structures on the local level. Therefore, the Defence's arguments that in some municipalities the civilian HVO was already the local government and it remained unchanged does not undermine the state of occupation. In some municipalities, such as Prozor, where there was still a legitimate local government alongside the HVO government, they were rendered incapable of functioning when the HVO military took over control with the attack. For example, in Prozor, with the attack on October -- 23 October 1992. The Chamber found that around 20 and 21 October 1992, so a few days before the attack, the Prozor municipal staff sent requests for assistance to Jablanica. Volume 2, paragraph 33, Exhibit 2D00061. On 23 October, the Prozor HVO president demanded that BiH Muslims immediately accept HVO political and military control. Volume 3, paragraph 38. When that did not happen, the HVO army assisted by the HV attacked Prozor town. Volume 3, paragraphs 38 through 41. And HVO thereafter occupied the town of Prozor from 22 to 30 October. In other areas, the Croats had already established political control before the Chamber found a state of occupation. Many were Croat-majority locations where the Croats had won the 1990 elections. The Defence argues that, in particular, in relation to Capljina, Ljubuski and Stolac, that this undermines a finding of occupation, that the Croats have the majority already before in these municipalities. But, Your Honours, winning the elections on the municipal level did not allow the Croats to replace the BiH municipal government with the local HVO government, a local government which is not accepted by and answering to the legitimate BiH government. I will address the facts in Capljina and Stolac in a bit more detail leaving aside Ljubuski because there are no findings on count 19, extensive destruction, in Ljubuski, and therefore it wouldn't have any impact. In relation to Capljina, the Defence pointed to the fact that the mayor of the municipality also became the president of the municipal HVO. This was correct. Moreover, until April 1993, the HVO and the ABiH fought side by side on the territory against Serb forces. Volume 2, paragraph 2053. But we have to consider what happened in April 1993. On 2 April 1993 an appeal for peace was signed by local leaders representing the Muslims in Capljina. Exhibit P01794. However, in April, the HVO arrested the Muslim men in Capljina including members of the ABiH, volume 3, paragraph 2075, which shows the Muslim representatives were disregarded. And, again, following Petkovic's order on the 30 June 1993, the HVO conducted a campaign of mass arrests of the Muslims in Capljina. Volume 2, paragraphs 2079, 2080. The finding that Capljina was occupied in July and through September 1993 was reasonable because the HVO exercised authority and the local BiH government was not able to function. Similarly, in Stolac, a Croat mayor was elected in the 1990 elections. Here, the Serbs controlled Stolac from April 1992. Volume 2, paragraph 1890. The Croat mayor left Stolac when the Serb army arrived in April 1992 and then resumed his responsibility once they left in mid-June 1992. Volume 2, paragraph 1890. On 1 July 1992, a Muslim Croat Crisis Staff was organised, volume 2, paragraph 1891, but after some time the Croats stopped co-operating and the Crisis Staff was replaced by the Stolac HVO. Volume 2, paragraph 1892. And then in April 1993, the HVO attempted to force the ABiH troops to leave the municipality, and on 19 April, the HVO disarmed and placed 183 members of the ABiH in detention. Volume 2, paragraph 1896. The finding that Stolac was occupied in July and August 1993 was therefore reasonable as the HVO had established authority in lieu of the local BiH government. To conclude, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber was reasonable in finding that occupation existed, based on the HVO's exercise of authority in the locations, its issuance of orders to the Muslim population, orders that were, in fact, followed. The mass arrests and displacements, the destruction and plunder of Muslim property show that the legitimate local government was not able to function. Stojic Ground 55 should be dismissed. Unless Your Honours have questions in relation to Ground 55, I would hand over the podium to Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You have exactly ten minutes remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This morning, Your Honours, the Defence failed to deal with Stojic himself. They didn't tell you who he was. They didn't talk about what he knew and they didn't talk about what he did. Stojic was not a political victim as the Defence have portrayed him this morning. As the head of the Defence Department, Stojic was a powerful figure who had the authority to hold HVO perpetrators accountable for the crimes they committed. Stojic knew about HVO crimes, but he allowed Muslims to be victimised over and over and over again by HVO forces. Stojic didn't just fail to hold perpetrators accountable, though, Your Honours. The Chamber reasonably found Stojic played a role in HVO operations in Gornji Vakuf, in Mostar, in Capljina, and in Vares, operations in which crimes were committed against Muslims. The HVO operations in West Mostar, which Stojic planned, resulted in mass arrests and expulsions of Muslims. As a result of these operations, thousands of Muslims were sent to East Mostar, where there was insufficient food, insufficient water, and insufficient medical care, where there was a daily and intense HVO shelling and sniping campaign, and where there was inadequate humanitarian aid because Stojic hindered the delivery of such aid. Stojic's involvement in HVO operations, the role he played in obstructing humanitarian aid, and his willingness to allow Muslims to be victimised by HVO forces over and over and over again demonstrates that the Chamber reasonably concluded that Stojic shared and significantly contributed to the common criminal purpose. In my submissions this afternoon, Your Honours, I'm going to begin by addressing Stojic's authority and then I'm going to deal with Stojic's shared intent and his contributions to the common criminal purpose, and when I do that, I'll address questions 4(c) and 8 in Your Honours' order for the preparation of the appeal hearing. I'll conclude, time permitting, by addressing Defence arguments concerning the existence, membership, and the ultimate purpose of the JCE. Turning then to Stojic's authority. He was, as I said, the head of the defence department, he was powerful, he had authority, and that authority is reflected in a variety of factors that the Chamber established. It's reflected in the high-level negotiations in which Stojic participated. It's reflected in the role Stojic played in formulating defence policy during HVO government meetings, but most of all, Your Honours, it is reflected in the control Stojic exercised over the armed forces, the military police, and HVO detention facilities. And I'll focus on Stojic's control over the armed forces and the military police. Your Honours, the Chamber's reasonable conclusion was that Stojic exercised command and effective control over the armed forces and the military police. Because he exercised effective control, Stojic had the material ability to prevent and punish their crimes. And there were a number of factors that the Chamber relied upon to establish Stojic's command and effective control. The Chamber's analysis is set out between paragraphs 299 and 320 of volume 4 of the judgement. What those factors show is that Stojic played a fundamental role in the establishment and organisation of the armed forces and the military police. He made high-level appointments within the armed forces and the military police. He designated members of the armed forces to participate in cease-fire negotiations. He was responsible for mobilising, arming, feeding, clothing and paying the armed forces and the military police. And he could tell members of the armed forces and the military police what to do by issuing orders to them, and they in turn kept him informed of what they were doing. All of those factors, Your Honours, show how broad Stojic's control was. All of those factors are consistent with the high-level position Stojic held within the military hierarchy. He was at the top. He was the member of government responsible for the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have four minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Main Staff and the military police administration were within his defence department. He could tell members of the armed forces and the military police what to do and he could control how they did it. He was the boss. Stojic's authority, Your Honours, was not narrow. The evidence the Chamber relied upon showed that he exercised broad control. The authority he possessed and exercised added up to one thing. It added up to command and effective control. This was a straightforward equation for the Chamber to solve and it solved it correctly. The Chamber reasonable concluded Stojic commanded and exercised control over the armed forces and the military police. I'm going to turn to Stojic's shared intent and contributions. I'm going to focus on Stojic's role in HVO operations and his failure to make a serious effort to stop crimes against Muslims. And I'm going to begin with the Gornji Vakuf operations which you heard about briefly this morning. What happened in Gornji Vakuf? Well, beginning on the 18th of January, 1993, the HVO violently attacked villages in Gornji Vakuf municipality, arrested Muslims and burnt down Muslim homes. The chamber reasonably concluded that Stojic planned the operations in Gornji Vakuf municipality. Why is the Chamber's conclusion reasonable? Four reasons, Your Honours. First, the operations in Gornji Vakuf municipality were carried out to enforce the government's 15 January ultimatum to the ABiH to subordinate to the HVO or leave Bosnian Croat-claimed territory. That's volume 4, paragraphs 125 to 127, 131, and 142. Second, Stojic was the one who was responsible for implementing that ultimatum. Volume 4, paragraph 304. Third, Stojic ordered Petkovic and Coric to implement the ultimatum. Volume 4, paragraph 304 as well. And, fourth, the Main Staff official whom Stojic sent to manage the situation in Gornji Vakuf, a man named Miro Andric, was the one who delivered ultimatum to ABiH representatives and ordered that force be used in the municipality after the ABiH rejected the ultimatum. That's volume 2, paragraphs 338 to 339, and 341, as well as volume 4, paragraphs 125 to 126. All of these signs point in one direction; they point to Stojic. And all these signs point to one answer about Stojic's role in the Gornji Vakuf operations; he played an important role. And in keeping with his deep involvement in those operations, Stojic reported on them to the government. Volume 4, paragraphs 127 and 300. Your Honours, if that is a convenient time. I will be moving on to question 4(c).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And we will reconvene this afternoon at 2.30 or quarter to 3.00. 2.45, you are correct, Judge Meron. 2.45. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.14 p.m. --- On at 2.44 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you may resume. And you have one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I continue, I just want to make a correction on the transcript. It's transcript page 68, line 2. There was a reference to the constitutional court decision, Exhibit P00505, and the correct date is September 1992, not September 1993. Again, it's September 1992. So I left off, Your Honours, talking about the Gornji Vakuf operations and the Chamber's finding concerning Stojic's involvement in those operations and that leads me to question 4(c) in Your Honours' order. And I'm going to address a part of that question. That part relates to Stojic's receipt of Zeljko Siljeg's report of the 28th and the 29th of January, 1993, Exhibit 1351. You've asked the parties to address the issue of who was privy to the contents of this particular report. The Chamber found that Stojic received this report as well as two other reports from Siljeg concerning the Gornji Vakuf operations. That's at paragraph 336 of volume 4. All three reports, Your Honours, Exhibits P1351, P1206, and P1357, contained information about violent crimes committed by the HVO during the Gornji Vakuf operations. And it was reasonable, Your Honours, for the Chamber to conclude that Stojic received these reports. The Defence have referred to the absence of a stamp. It doesn't show otherwise. It doesn't show that the Chamber was unreasonable to conclude that Stojic received those three reports. Why was it reasonable? I'm going to give you four reasons why it was reasonable. Reason 1, Siljeg's reports were addressed to Stojic's Defence Department. Reason 2, Stojic was deeply involved in the operations that were discussed in the reports. Refer you back to my earlier submissions concerning the ultimatum and his role in implementing that ultimatum. Reason 3, there was a system, Your Honours, within the HVO which depended upon Stojic receiving information about military operations because he had a responsibility to provide the government with information about the military situation on the ground. I refer Your Honours to volume 4, paragraphs 91 and 300. And reason 4, Stojic clearly was receiving information about the Gornji Vakuf operations because he updated the government about those operations. Volume 4, paragraph 127. So, Your Honours, the Prosecution submission is that the Chamber reasonably concluded that Stojic received Exhibit P1351 as well as Exhibits P1206 and P1357. I'm going to move on to Mostar, another operation in which Stojic played a very important role. HVO operations in West Mostar, Your Honours, began on 9th of May, 1993, and they continued throughout Stojic's participation in the JCE. Beginning on 9th of May, between 1500 and 2500 Muslims, men, women, children, and elderly, were forced out of their homes and taken to Heliodrom detention centre. While many Muslims were allowed to return to their homes, this was just temporary. Because by the end of May 1993, Muslims were being forced from their homes and across the confrontation line into East Mostar. And these expulsions, they continued in June 1993, they continued in July 1993, they continued in August 1993. As the Chamber's analysis in volume 2 demonstrates, the expulsions continued throughout Stojic's participation in implementing the common criminal purpose. What took place in West Mostar was organised violence. Organised violence that the Chamber reasonably concluded Stojic participated in planning. Now in Grounds 31 and 33 of their appeal the Defence challenge that conclusion. They haven't discussed it this morning but they have challenged it in Grounds 31 and 33 of their appeal. But, Your Honours, when the evidence that the Chamber relied upon is considered together, pieces of evidence that it relied upon fit together as neatly as pieces of a puzzle, a puzzle that shows that Stojic participated in planning the West Mostar eviction operations. Now there are four pieces to this puzzle. I'm going to take you through those four pieces. Piece number one is the evidence showing that Stojic presented himself to the outside world as if he had played a role in planning the operations in Mostar. When Stojic spoke to the BBC in May 1993, and international representatives on 17th July 1993, he spoke as if he was intimately familiar with HVO objectives and the means by which those objectives would be achieved in Mostar. Volume 4, paragraphs 346, 348, 353, and 361. He presented himself as if he had played a role in planning those operations. Piece number two. Piece number two is Stojic's high-level position. This is piece number two because the way Stojic presented himself when speaking to the BBC in May 1993 and with international representatives on 17 July 1993 was consistent with his leadership role. It was Stojic's job to know what the armed forces were going to do in Mostar. And the other pieces of this puzzle, pieces three and four, confirmed that the way Stojic presented himself was the way things actually were. Piece number three are the reports Stojic received relating to the HVO's eviction operations in West Mostar, reports the Defence claim Stojic never received. That's in Ground 33 of their appeal. But the reports were personally addressed to Stojic. On 14 June 1993, Stojic received a report informing him that evictions in West Mostar were accompanied by killings, beatings and rapes. That report is discussed at paragraph 351 of volume 4 and paragraphs 868 and 870 of volume 2. On the 5 July, 1993, another report was sent to Stojic, a report listing the homes of Muslim families to be raided. A report the Chamber relied upon to conclude that expulsion operations were organised and carried out building by building in West Mostar. A report sent to Stojic personally to keep him informed of the progress of the eviction operations and that report is discussed at paragraph 897 of volume 2 and paragraph 352 of volume 4. Your Honours, as Muslims were evicted from flats in Mostar, those flats were assigned to members of the HVO armed forces and the military police as well as Croatian families who arrived from other municipalities. That's from paragraphs 824, 827, and 876 of volume 2; and paragraph 929 of volume 4. And Stojic received information about this component of the eviction operation as well. Exhibit P2608, which the Chamber discussed at paragraph 351 of volume 4, is a report that Stojic received on the 2nd of June, 1993, in which he was informed that members of the Ludvig Pavlovic Special Purposes Unit had occupied vacated flats in Mostar. Your Honours, beyond the reports Stojic received concerning the expulsion operations in West Mostar, beyond his high-level position and beyond the way in which Stojic presented himself, there's Witness DZ's evidence, and this is piece number four of the puzzle. Witness DZ's evidence was that Mate Boban's assistant, and you will recall that Mate Boban was the president of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban's assistant Vladimir Pogarcic identified Stojic as the one in charge of the ethnic cleansing campaign 234 in Mostar. Volume 4, paragraph 354. Witness DZ's well-corroborated evidence is another piece of the puzzle, Your Honours, that fits just right. The Chamber concluded that Stojic participated in planning the expulsion operations in West Mostar. Chamber also found that Stojic played a role in HVO operations in Capljina and Vares. I won't be addressing those operations. We rely on the arguments in our response brief. I want to move on, Your Honours, to Stojic's failure to stop crimes against Muslims. Stojic had the authority to repress crime by HVO forces but he didn't do anything. And the Chamber reasonably relied on that finding to conclude that Stojic shared and significantly contributed to the common criminal purpose. Stojic never issued meaningful orders to halt the crimes against Muslims. His high-level position gave him a platform from which he could condemn crimes. Stojic condemned crimes against Croats. You have an example of that at paragraph 421 of volume 4. But Stojic never spoke out when it came to crimes against Muslims. He did the opposite. He denied HVO responsibility and commended and praised known perpetrators. And in that way, Stojic allowed HVO perpetrators to continue victimising Muslims. Stojic was certainly well-informed of crimes against Muslims. The Chamber's reasonable finding shows Stojic received reports of HVO crimes from internal channels within the HVO. He also received information from international representatives, international representatives who approached Stojic to discuss their concerns about the eviction of Muslims, volume 4, paragraph 350; who spoke to Stojic about the shelling and sniping campaign being carried out against East Mostar, volume 4, paragraph 359, 367, and 748 to 749; and international representatives who approached Stojic to secure access to East Mostar so that humanitarian aid could be delivered to the population that was trapped there, volume 2, paragraph 1236. Yet despite all that he knew, Stojic failed to make a serious effort to stop crimes against Muslims. Now, in their brief, Defence have argued that the Chamber was wrong to reach that conclusion and that's at -- those are Grounds 23.3 and 33.2. I'm going give you four examples, Your Honours, which demonstrate that the Chamber was right. Stojic failed to make a serious effort to stop crimes against Muslims. Example one. Stojic never dealt with the crimes he learned of at the Heliodrom or other HVO detention facilities. Volume 4, paragraphs 395 to 396 and 407. As far as the Heliodrom is concerned, Stojic received a lot of information concerning the terrible conditions at that facility. Now this is Exhibit P4352. This is just one of the reports that Stojic received concerning the Heliodrom. There were other reports. Those are discussed at paragraphs 388 and 391 to 392 of volume 4. This report was sent to Stojic on 20 August 1993 by the Heliodrom warden, Stanko Bozic. In Ground 37 of their appeal, the Defence argue that Stojic never received this report, but, Your Honours, it was reasonable for the Chamber to conclude that he did because the report is personally addressed to Stojic. This is an excerpt from page 1 of the report and, as you can see, Bozic refers to the ICRC's objections concerning the use of detainees for forced labour and the poor conditions of confinement at the Heliodrom. This is an excerpt from page 2 of the report where Bozic says that: "After the Red Cross's departure, we were not able to remedy these wrong-doings. On the contrary, the number of wounded and killed at the workplace is increasing by the day." He asks Stojic to "please help us to resolve this problem." Did Stojic try and resolve the problems at the Heliodrom? Did he order that Muslims who were unlawfully detained be released and allowed to return to their homes? The Chamber found that Stojic had the power to do that at paragraph 915 of volume 1. Did he order that the conditions at the Heliodrom be improved? Did he insist that detainees not be taken to perform dangerous work on the front lines? No, he didn't. He didn't do any of those things. He took no measures to rectify the situation at the Heliodrom. That's at paragraph 395 of volume 4. Stojic didn't do anything about these crimes because he had no intention of stopping crimes against Muslims. Example two. Chamber reasonably found that Stojic exercised control over HVO snipers in Mostar. Stojic controlled HVO snipers, knew they were targeting civilians in East Mostar and he allowed it to happen. Volume 4, paragraphs 365 and 368 to 370. He allowed it to happen because he had no intention of stopping crimes against Muslims. Example three. Stojic lied to international representatives when they confronted him about HVO involvement in evictions in West Mostar. On the 16th of June, 1993, Stojic met with ECMM representatives who told him about the evictions taking place in West Mostar and told him that the HVO was responsible for those evictions. Volume 4, paragraphs 350 and 422. Now, two days before that meeting, Stojic received this report and this is Exhibit P2770. I mentioned this report when I spoke about Stojic's involvement in the West Mostar expulsion campaign. As you can see, the original B/C/S language version appears on the right side and the English translation appears on the left. Chamber found at paragraphs 868 and 870 of volume 2 and paragraphs 351 and 416 of volume 4 that Stojic received this report on the 14th of June, 1993. You see Stojic's -- you see Stojic's first name Bruno at the upper right-hand side of the document. The Defence challenges the Chamber's finding that Stojic received this document in Ground 33 of their appeal. But, Your Honours it was addressed to Stojic personally so it was reasonable for the Chamber to conclude that he received it. And in addition to the fact that the report was personally addressed to Stojic, the Chamber heard witness testimony confirming that Stojic received reports generated by the HVO Main Staff's electronic operations centre, the CED. That's at paragraph 870 of volume 2 and paragraph 736 of volume 1. Your Honours, the CED was responsible for preparing this report. As you can see, that abbreviation appears on the upper left-hand side of the document. Stojic received this report. And this is -- this slide magnifies the text of that report. And as can see, the report refers to events in the Dum neighbourhood of West Mostar. The report refers to evictions of Muslims, forceable moves into apartments, rapes, beatings, maltreatment, and "indications of new murders of civilians." And the report refers to the perpetrators who are members of the HVO. Now, it's important to remember, Your Honours, that in addition to this report, it's important to remember that Stojic wasn't sitting in some far away place when the expulsion campaign in West Mostar was taking place. He was in the thick of it. He was based in West Mostar. And the relevant citations on that are collected at paragraph 261 of our response brief. Stojic knew about the violent evictions in West Mostar but yet despite what he knew, Stojic told ECMM representatives that the HVO wasn't involved. Stojic lied to ECMM representatives because he had no intention of stopping crimes against crimes. That takes me to example four. Stojic praised and commended Mladen Naletilic's troops although he knew they were responsible for evictions and violent crimes in West Mostar. Naletilic, Your Honours will recall, was convicted by this Tribunal. He was the commander of a military formation called the Convicts Battalion. It's volume 1, paragraph 817. In August 1993, Stojic told a SpaBat official that he had confidence in Naletilic's Convicts Battalion because they were well trained. Volume 4, paragraph 418. In September 1993, Stojic officially commended Naletilic and his Convicts Battalion. Also volume 4, paragraph 418. Stojic delivered his praise and commendation although he knew that members of Naletilic's Convicts Battalion were responsible for crimes against Muslims in West Mostar. I want to take you back to the report from 14th of June, 1993, Exhibit P2770, that I just showed you a moment ago. Who were the perpetrators of the crimes documented in the report? The report, as you can see, identifies Vinko Martinovic who was convicted with Naletilic at this Tribunal. Martinovic was the commander of the Vinko Skrobo anti-terrorist group which was under Naletilic's command volume 1, paragraph 818. The other named perpetrators in the report were members of the Vinko Skrobo unit. Volume 4, paragraph 416. So Stojic knew that members of Naletilic's Convicts Battalion were responsible for crimes in West Mostar as of June 1993, yet he praised and commended them a few months later. Stojic praised and commended them because he had no intention of stopping crimes against Muslims. He wanted to encourage perpetrators to continue committing crimes, and he succeeded in doing that because members of Tuta's Convicts Battalion, Naletilic's Convicts Battalion, continued to victimise Muslims in West Mostar throughout Stojic's participation in the JCE. That's volume 2, paragraphs 980 to 982, 984, and 986 to 987. Now, on Ground s 23.1 and 23.3 of their appeal, the Defence has argued that crime couldn't be effectively opposed and so for that reason the Chamber was wrong to find that Stojic didn't make a serious effort to stop crime. Your Honours, this wasn't a situation where the prevailing circumstances prevented Stojic from acting to put a stop to the awful things that were happening to Muslims. This was a situation where Stojic created the conditions in which Muslims were victimised and then made the situation worse through inaction, lies, and encouragement to perpetrators. I'm just wondering, Your Honour, how many time I have left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have -- 36 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I wanted to turn to Your Honours' questions now. I want to address question 8 in Your Honours' order for the preparation of the appeal hearing. Your Honours have asked whether in convicting Stojic, Praljak, and Petkovic of the crime of unlawful infliction of terror on civilians under Count 25 of the indictment, the Trial Chamber made the necessary findings in relation to their specific intent to spread terror among civilian population and what the impact would be if the Appeals Chamber found that the Trial Chamber failed to provide a reasoned opinion in this regard. I'll deal with that question as it pertains to Stojic. Your Honours, I'm not going to stand up here and tell you that the Chamber made an explicit finding that Stojic possessed the specific intent to spread terror. Because it didn't, it didn't make an explicit finding. But this judgement, like any other trial judgement, needs to be read as a whole. And in his submissions this morning, Mr. Khan ignored that. Paragraphs 468 and 470 of the Djordjevic appeal judgement stand for that very proposition. And on the issue of whether Stojic possessed the specific intent to spread terror, there's only one reasonable reading of the judgement when it's read as a whole. And that one reasonable reading is that it is inherent in the judgement that Stojic possessed the specific intent to spread terror. It's inherent because the Chamber's findings read as a whole demonstrate that Stojic was heavily involved in the Mostar operations. Stojic, Your Honours, was so heavily involved that when the Chamber found that the HVO possessed the specific intent to spread terror at paragraph 1692 of volume 3, one of the people within the HVO that the Chamber must have been referring to was Stojic. And when the Chamber found that Stojic shared the common criminal purpose and held him responsible for the crime of terror at paragraphs 428 and 431 of volume 4, the Chamber had clearly satisfied itself that Stojic possessed the specific intent to spread terror. So what it comes down to, Your Honours, in the Prosecution's submission, are the findings which show that Stojic was heavily involved in the Mostar operations. So let me tell you about those findings. Stojic exercised effective control over the forces that shelled and sniped at East Mostar day after day until his participation in the JCE ended. He not only controlled those forces. He knew exactly what they were doing. He knew because he received reports from international representatives. Relevant evidence is cited at paragraph 359 of volume 4. He knew because he spoke to international representatives about the plan of action for Mostar. Based on Stojic's remarks, international representatives surmised that the attacks, the deprivation, and the isolation in East Mostar would force the Muslims of East Mostar out of Mostar entirely. Volume 4, paragraph 362, and volume 2, paragraph 1246. Your Honours, that was enough to establish Stojic's knowledge of what was taking place in East Mostar. But on top of the reports and on top of the remarks about the plan in Mostar, as I mentioned earlier, Stojic was based in West Mostar, he had a front-row seat for the horror show taking place in East Mostar, and yet despite all that he knew, Stojic allowed shelling and sniping attacks to take place. And he didn't just allow the attacks to take place. Stojic aggravated the terrible situation in East Mostar. How did he do that? He aggravated the situation in East Mostar by planning expulsions of Muslims from West to East Mostar, talked about those expulsions, expulsions which provided HVO forces with more and more civilians to target and terrorise. And he aggravated the situation in East Mostar by obstructing the delivery of humanitarian aid to East Mostar which exacerbated the deprivation and the misery which prevailed there. Volume 2, paragraph 1231, and volume 4, paragraph 372. So, Your Honours, that takes me back to where I began with the answer. The inescapable conclusion when the findings related to Stojic are read as a whole is that when the Chamber says at paragraph 1692 of volume 3 that the HVO possessed the specific intent for terror, one of the people within the HVO that the Chamber must have been referring to was Stojic. And when the Chamber found Stojic shared the intent for the common criminal purpose and found him responsible for the crime of terror, the Chamber clearly satisfied itself that Stojic possessed the specific intent for terror. That's the only way to read this judgement given the findings that the Chamber made about Stojic's role in the events in Mostar. And when it is inherent in the judgement that a finding has been made as it is in this instance, that's sufficient. But if Your Honours find that the Chamber failed to provide a reasoned opinion, then Your Honours shouldn't leave Stojic's responsibility for the crime of terror unadjudicated. The Prosecution would urge you to review the findings in the judgement and the evidence on the record, and when you do that, you'll reach the same inescapable conclusion that we say is inherent in the judgement, that Stojic possessed the specific intent for terror. I want to move on, Your Honours, to the Defence's factual challenges relating to the existence of the common criminal purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: May I ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Counsel, I don't have the case in front of me. But I seem to recall that in the Galic appeal judgement we dealt specifically with the modalities of specific intent in the context of the crime of terror under customary law, and Article 51, paragraph 2, of Additional Protocol I. I also believe that the Appeals Chamber went to considerable lengths to attribute the intent to the specific accused rather than attributing to a force. I have listened carefully to you, but you are saying that, well, if the Trial Chamber forgot to do it or didn't do it is the job of the Appeals Chamber, which, of course, did not listen to the whole evidence so we should make a finding of specific intent if the Trial Chamber did not. And if the Appeals Chamber is not persuaded, and I'm not suggesting that it will not be, but if is not persuaded by your sort of holistic attitude by saying the force must have acted pursuant to intent, so Mr. Stojic must be a part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you want me to respond to that, Your Honour? My response is that simply that it is well established in the jurisprudence that judgements do need to be read as a whole, and what we are saying is that this particular finding is inherent in the judgement. It is inherent in different places, it's inherent in the finding in volume 3, and it's inherent in the finding that Stojic shared the common criminal purpose and what -- the Prosecution's submission is that when you put everything together, that it is abundantly clear it -- it is inherent that the Chamber has satisfied itself that Stojic possessed the specific intent for terror. But if Your Honours are not persuaded, then the task of evaluating the findings and the evidence is a practice that the Appeals Chamber has regularly engaged in in order to make findings where it has been unsatisfied that a Trial Chamber has made the appropriate finding, and so we do not think there would be any unfairness or there would be a divergence from practice to do so in this particular instance. That's the Prosecution's submission. If there are no other questions, I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honours, I'm going to turn now, as I said, to the Defence's factual challenges relating to the existence of the common criminal purpose. None of the arguments that the Defence have made confront the Chamber's analysis. They've spoken about it at length, but they haven't confronted what the Chamber found and the basis on which the Chamber found what it did. At the heart of the Chamber's analysis, Your Honours, was the very obvious pattern of criminal activity targeted at Muslims during and after HVO operations, a pattern that began following the government's ultimatum to the ABiH on 15 January 1993 and the ensuing attacks and crimes in Gornji Vakuf municipality. From mid-January 1993 until April 1994, across Herceg-Bosna, the HVO carried out violent attacks targeting Muslim civilians, evicted Muslims from their homes, arrested Muslims en masse, mistreated Muslims in detention, expelled Muslims to ABiH-held territory, and by the summer of 1993, used release from detention as a means of expelling Muslims to third countries. This wasn't a question of some criminal acts as the Defence indicated this morning. This was a pattern of crime that resulted in the depletion of the Muslim population. As the Chamber observed at paragraph 57 of volume 4, between September and October 1993, the Muslim population of Ljubuski municipality went from 2381 to 826, the Muslim population of Capljina municipality went from 14085 to 3852, and the Muslim population of Stolac municipality from 8093 to 0. Now, the pattern of HVO crimes against Muslims was at the centre of the Chamber's analysis, but it was also complemented by the organised influx of Croats into Herceg-Bosna. The Chamber's conclusion that there was a common criminal purpose wasn't just about this two-way process, though, this two-way process of removing Muslims from Herceg-Bosna and bringing Croats into Herceg-Bosna because the process of changing Herceg-Bosna's ethnic composition also aligned with the statements that JCE members made. Mate Boban's statement at the 27 December 1991 presidential meeting, which my learned colleague referred to this morning, she referred to that transcript, that was a meeting with Croatian President Franjo Tudjman and others just over a month after the creation of Herceg-Bosna where Boban spoke of "cleansing border areas" of Herceg-Bosna to increase the size of Herceg-Bosna's Croatian population. That's from pages 34 to 35 of Exhibit P89 which is cited in footnote 120 of volume 4. And two weeks later, Tudjman referred to population exchanges in a meeting with a Bosnian Serb leader. That's Exhibit P108, pages 31 to 33 and 41 to 42. At 26 September 1992 presidential meeting with Tudjman and other Croat leaders, Praljak indicated in reference to Muslim refugees in Herceg-Bosna that "it would be difficult to make those people leave those parts in any way and unless we evict those people from there, we will not have a majority there." Volume 4, paragraph 522. At a 26 October 1992 meeting with VRS Main Staff chief Ratko Mladic, a meeting at which Prlic, Stojic, and Petkovic were present, Praljak stated: "It is in our interest that the Muslims get their own canton so they have somewhere to move to." That's from page 3 of Exhibit P11380 which is relied on upon at paragraph 43 of volume 4. Your Honours, beyond these statements, the process of removing Muslims from Herceg-Bosna and bringing Croats into Herceg-Bosna aligned with the goal that Franjo Tudjman and other JCE members shared of imposing Croat control over as much as of the Banovina as possible because as the Chamber recognised at paragraph 43 of volume 4, Croat dominance over the Banovina could only be achieved by changing Herceg-Bosna's ethnic composition. The Defence referred to the finding at paragraph 43 as a vague finding. It was no vague finding. I used this analogy earlier, Your Honours, but it applies here as well. The pieces just fit together, they fit together like a puzzle, and the Defence haven't shown otherwise. Now, the Defence have a referred to co-operation between the HVO and the ABiH. They say this co-operation is inconsistent with the existence of a common criminal purpose. Yes, the HVO and the ABiH did co-operate in fighting the VRS. The Prosecution has never said otherwise. But despite this co-operation, JCE members still had a vision of creating a Croat-dominated entity spanning the Banovina borders. JCE members still spoke of removing Muslims from Herceg-Bosna. JCE members still committed horrific crimes against Muslims across Herceg-Bosna, crimes that depleted Herceg-Bosna of its Muslim population. And the HVO still tried to repopulate Herceg-Bosna with Croats. Co-operation between the HVO and the ABiH doesn't undermine the Chamber's conclusion that there was a common criminal purpose. Now, we've addressed much of the evidence that the Defence referred to this morning in our response brief. I just want to address a couple of exhibits that they referred to. In relation to Exhibit 2D1107, the Defence suggested that this exhibit showed that the HVO provided material and weapons to the ABiH in Mostar in May 1993. It did not. This exhibit shows that the HVO approved the transport of material and weapons to the ABiH in northern Bosnia where there was -- where there were confrontations with the VRS. I refer Your Honours to Exhibit 2D1107 as well as Exhibit 2D1108 and the testimony of Makar at transcript pages 38447 to 38449. The Defence told you that Exhibit 2D959 shows further material and weapon delivery by the HVO to the ABiH in August 1993. 2D959 was not admitted and, in any event, the document does not show the ABiH received the weapons referred to in the report. The document shows the end point of the transit of weapons is the HVO's logistic base in Grude. Now, the Defence this morning challenged the Chamber's conclusion that the common criminal purpose was established by mid-January 1993, but again they ignore the Chamber's analysis. The Chamber made it clear that the JCE members relied on their interpretation of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan to implement the common criminal purpose. Volume 4, paragraphs 44 and 65. The government's 15 January ultimatum which Stojic ordered Coric and Petkovic to implement, which I referred to earlier, contained the -- contained the JCE members interpretation of Vance-Owen. Volume 4, paragraph 139 to 140. And this interpretation of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was enforced through a campaign of ethnic cleansing that began in Gornji Vakuf municipality immediately after the 15 January ultimatum was issued and occurred again and again and again throughout Herceg-Bosna. It was reasonable, Your Honours, for the Chamber to conclude that the common criminal purpose had formed by mid-January 1993. Now, this morning the Defence broadly challenged the ultimate purpose conclusion. Defence say presidential transcripts don't support the Chamber's conclusion. They do. The ultimate purpose section of the judgement in volume 4 is filled with evidence from presidential transcripts and the evidence of international witnesses which clearly show that the Chamber's conclusion concerning the ultimate purpose was reasonable. Now, Mr. Khan showed you a few transcripts and said, well, look, there is an inconsistency between what Chamber found and what the evidence says. But there's no inconsistency. I'm going to give you one example. The Defence referred to Exhibit P2466. Defence said that, look, this 20 May 1993 internal meeting, Tudjman allegedly argued against the escalation of conflict between the Muslims because this would endanger the interests of the Croat state because he was worried about sanctions. That's at page 11. What Mr. Khan didn't tell you was that the page before, page 10, on page 10, Tudjman said: "I said to Izetbegovic in private in Split before the meeting, that this, what they are doing by starting the conflict with Croats and trying to conquer part of the area, the provinces led and controlled by Croatia is suicidal politics for the Muslims. Croats cannot agree to lose areas that used to be part of the Banovina of Croatia." The evidence the Defence refers to you is just further proof of ultimate purpose, the ultimate purpose to create a Croat-dominated entity in Bosnia-Herzegovina spanning the Banovina borders. This morning the Defence challenged the Chamber's conclusion that Franjo Tudjman, Croatian Defence Minister Gojko Susak and Croatian Army Chief of Staff Janko Bobetko were JCE members. Your Honours, the first point I want to make is that Stojic's JCE responsibility doesn't depend on the finding that Tudjman, Susak, and Bobetko were JCE members as the Defence have argued. Regardless of whether these three men were JCE members, the Chamber's finding that there was a plurality of persons who share the common criminal purpose would stand, and the crimes imputed through the JCE would remain unchanged, JCE crimes were imputed through the appellants, not through Tudjman, Susak or Bobetko. Volume 4, paragraph 1232. But having said that, Your Honours, the Chamber made absolutely no error in naming Tudjman, Susak, and Bobetko as JCE members. The Chamber found at paragraph 1222 of volume 4 that Tudjman, Susak, and Bobetko directly collaborated with the HVO leadership to further the JCE. Your Honours, there is no error in that finding because that finding is an understatement. Let me explain why. I'll begin with Tudjman and then I'll deal with Susak and Bobetko. Tudjman's vision of a Croat entity in Bosnia-Herzegovina encompassing the Banovina borders, a vision he shared with the other JCE members, was the driving force behind the common criminal purpose. Tudjman knew this vision could only be achieved by changing Herceg-Bosna's ethnic composition by moving Muslims out and bringing Croats in. The Chamber found as much at paragraph 43 of volume 4. We've already referred to that finding. And so, Your Honours, as we've argued in our brief in response to Grounds 6 and 14 of Stojic's appeal, when Tudjman planned HVO operations, when he strategised with HVO leaders on political and military matters, and when he shaped Herceg-Bosna's political and military leadership structure, he was doing these things to advance the JCE. Tudjman wasn't silent as the Defence have suggested. He led. As he planned and strategised with the HVO, Tudjman repeatedly acknowledged the horrific crimes by the HVO against Muslims. And for that, I would refer Your Honours to the testimony of the former US ambassador to Croatia, Peter Galbraith, testimony the Chamber cited at paragraph 562 of volume 3. What you have, then, Your Honours, is the combination of Tudjman's repeated acknowledgment that the HVO were committing crimes against Muslims and the continued direction which Tudjman provided to the HVO to accomplish this project of creating a Croat-dominated Herceg-Bosna. The combination of those factors demonstrates that the Chamber reasonably concluded that Tudjman was a JCE member. But that wasn't the only support for this conclusion. According to Ambassador Galbraith, Tudjman believed "states ought to be ethnically homogeneous." And Tudjman expressed his support for population exchanges. Transcript pages 6429 and 6435. The very sort of exchange that Boban and Prlic tried to carry out in early May 1993. Muslims from Mostar for Croats from Central Bosnia. As you heard from Mr. Stringer yesterday, the international organisation that Boban and Prlic sought assistance from to carry out this exchange refused to become involved in an attempt by HVO leaders to create "ethnically homogeneous zones." The organisation communicated its refusal to Tudjman and Boban on 12th of May. Volume 4, paragraph 54. By then, the HVO had already moved on from population exchange to mass arrests and ultimately ethnically cleansing Muslims from West Mostar. Evidence of Tudjman's JCE membership doesn't end there, though. Tudjman welcomed the demographic changes that took place in Herceg-Bosna. At a meeting on 21 September 1993 at his presidential palace, Tudjman was told by Stolac's HVO president, Andjelko Markovic that: "Stolac was twice defended as you once said, once from the Muslims and from the Chetniks. Today there is not a single Muslim in Stolac. We have populated Stolac with our refugees from Bosnia." Tudjman's immediate reaction was to say: "Andjelko, I know all that." And to later comment that it had been his idea to populate Stolac with Croats. That's from pages 4 and 17 to 18 of Exhibit P5237. That exhibit is cited and discussed at paragraph 2034 of volume 2. Tudjman's reaction demonstrates that what he heard had happened to the Muslims of Stolac was what he expected to hear. Now, in their appeal brief, the Defence referred to Tudjman's reaction to the crimes in Stupni Do and the destruction of the old bridge. But that evidence, Your Honours, provides more proof of Tudjman's JCE membership. As we've argued in our response brief at paragraph 51, Tudjman's only concern was the international scrutiny these crimes attracted. Tudjman wasn't generally interested in holding perpetrators accountable or in stopping the ethnic cleansing campaign. If Tudjman had really been in interesting in stopping the ethnic cleansing campaign, he wouldn't have said that Ivica Rajic whose troops physically perpetrated the crimes in Stupni Do could continue serving in the HVO in Gornji Vakuf. Volume 3, paragraph 564. He wouldn't have accepted the forced removal of all of Stolac's Muslim population, and on a broader level, he wouldn't have planned HVO operations and strategised with HVO leaders for months and months while at the same time acknowledging the horrific crimes HVO members were committing.
