The Chamber reasonably concluded that Tudjman was a JCE member. What about Susak and Bobetko? Susak and Bobetko implemented Tudjman's policies in Herceg-Bosna. Tudjman directed them to work with the HVO to achieve his objectives. That's evident from a number of the presidential transcripts that we've cited in Grounds 6 and 14 of our response brief. There is one in particular I'd like to highlight. This is an excerpt from page 54 of Exhibit P3112 which is a presidential transcript of the 2nd of July, 1993. Incorrect date as it appears on the slide. It is, in fact, the 2nd of July. These are Tudjman's words. Tudjman says: "But at the same time we must take steps to protect Croatian interests in the territorial sense, too. And you two, please, Minister Susak, General Bobetko, see about this and meet with Herceg-Bosna leaders there, with General Praljak, Petkovic, and Ambassador Sancevic and their leaders there, with Boban and Prlic, to discuss exactly what should be done. But it goes without saying, do not lead the operation in such a way as to make it a direct involvement." This, as I said, was on the 2nd of July, 1993. After the crimes in Gornji Vakuf municipalities, after the crimes in Jablanica municipality, after the crimes in Prozor municipality, after the expulsion campaign in West Mostar had begun, after the siege of East Mostar had begun, and just as the mass arrest operation across Herceg-Bosna was taking place. The presidential transcripts that we've cited in our response brief demonstrate the Susak and Bobetko provided direction to the HVO as its members committed horrific crimes against Muslims. So, Your Honours, for that reason the Chamber reasonably concluded that Susak and Bobetko were JCE members as well. Before I conclude, Your Honours, I just want to address briefly, very briefly, a point the Defence made about the Mladic diaries this is morning. Now, the inference that the Chamber drew from the Mladic diaries is at paragraph 43 of volume 4, relied on those diaries to conclude that by October 1992, Prlic, Stojic, Petkovic, and Praljak knew that achieving the ultimate purpose would involve Muslims moving out of Herceg-Bosna. That was a reasonable finding to make given the nature of the comments that Praljak -- that are attributed to Praljak in those diaries. Now, this morning, Mr. Khan said that the Mladic diaries were the foundation of the majority finding that Stojic was linked as an individual to the JCE. That position is elaborated upon in the appeal brief at paragraph 132, the Defence said that this is the only finding in relation to Stojic's knowledge of the common purpose of the JCE and without this finding the conviction of Stojic for participation in the JCE could not stand. Your Honours, prior knowledge of the JCE isn't a legal ingredient for JCE liability. The finding that Stojic knew that the ultimate purpose would involve Muslims moving out the Herceg-Bosna was relevant to establishing the Chamber's conclusion that there was a common criminal purpose and that Stojic shared that purpose. It was a reasonable finding, very well-supported finding, but it wasn't decisive. Your Honours, those are my submissions, unless you have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Whenever counsel states it fits just right, one's ears should prick up and one should be very vigilant. It fits just right. Pieces of a puzzle cut almost to order. That's the tenor of the Prosecution's response. And I will pause and say it was within the last ten minutes or 15 minutes when the Prosecution really started addressing or seeking to address the main planks of the submissions put forward by Bruno Stojic in our oral argument today. Of course, very interesting about international armed conflict and occupation, but we had written briefs. It was their decision to focus on that but they heard full well the way I put the case this morning. They had every opportunity to seek to decimate the argument that I postulated on behalf of Mr. Bruno Stojic. Rather than do that, they sought to squeeze in some kind of repost, the Mladic diaries, in extra time. We say that's quite significant. Fits just right. Judge Antonetti in his dissent states at page 67: "I deeply regret that, in my view, the Prosecution had a very selective approach to its documents, retaining only those supporting its arguments and setting aside all those likely to compromise it's point of view. I do not think this is the most efficient practice to adopt with regards to crimes falling under international humanitarian law." And he goes on. The Prosecution, in my respectful submission, have done little more than regurgitate the arguments that they presented before the Trial Chamber, and then add a caveat: The Trial Chamber agreed, the Trial Chamber found, it's all very reasonable. Well, that's not a proper response. It is circuitous. The test isn't whether a decision is reasonable, whether or not a hypothesis could reasonable be constructed. Despite me saying, I hoped quite clearly today, that the test is whether or not -- because it is a case based upon inference upon circumstantial evidence which can be compelling. The old adage that it is like a rope, that one strand is not enough to sustain it, but many strands together may be enough to sustain a conviction comes to mind. But when there are other reasonable explanations, other reasonable conclusions, that is highly relevant to a criminal case. And my learned friend was quite -- the Prosecution didn't address those key arguments. Perhaps I was unclear when I dealt with 2D1107. The document was absolutely accurately presented by me. The key to that document wasn't where the MTS went. It was my reference to Makar, the witness Makar, that he collected that ordinance, those fire-arms in Mostar. Now we were trying until we were blue in the face to make the Prosecution understand that one doesn't give a fire-arms -- to use an analogy, one doesn't give a gun to one's enemy in one's own home in the belief that they're going to use it outside. So the fact that weapons were given in Mostar to what the Prosecution said at that time were the enemy was highly relevant. It shed light on whether or not there was an intent, whether or not there was a JCE with an ultimate purpose or whether or not that was simply an ambitious construction by the Prosecution. Your Honour, in relation to question 4, I will discuss again the documents P1351 and 3D0365. The reason the majority found or gave weight to P1351 is apparent in the judgement at paragraph 355 -- 355 -- 335, page 116. Now, with your leave, let's look at firstly, once again, 3D0365. The Trial Chamber, we say, unreasonably cited this document as evidence of intent of Bruno Stojic in relation to the Prosecution counts of crimes, murder, in Gornji Vakuf. But let's look at it. Firstly I point out, because it is relevant when you go to the next document, it is addressed to Bruno Stojic. We have seen other documents on the screen today by the Prosecution with "Bruno Stojic" typed in. First paragraph, Miro Andric says in his report dated the 27th of January is that he went often a mission to Prozor with the objective of calming the situation in Gornji Vakuf municipality. Not incitement, not violence, not military engagement to calm it down. 12th of January. Down the page he has a meeting on the 13th of January. "Following the instructions I had received," he says, "that the differences had to be resolved peacefully," "peacefully" staring the Prosecution in the face, "peacefully and by negotiations," not by guns, not by fire, not by belligerency, and yet the Judges bought -- the majority bought the Prosecution's line that this was somehow an incriminating document. Your Honour, on the second page, page 3 in fact, the letter further states: "On 18th of January, following an order from our superiors, it was decided to use force to exert pressure on the OS BH," so on and so forth. Your Honours have agreed and granted leave in your decision of the 11th of March that that translation was wrong and instead it was to be replaced with "following a higher order." So when one looks at this document from Mr. Andric addressed to Bruno Stojic in which he relates orders given by Bruno Stojic and looks at the construction of the properly translated document "following a higher order," it seems plain, in our respectful submission, that the higher order does not come from Bruno Stojic. It doesn't say from you, from the head of the Defence Department. So the conclusion that this document somehow is incriminatory is patently unfair. In fact it's exculpatory. It's exculpatory. And despite that, we say the Trial Chamber unreasonably characterised this as an incriminatory document and because they viewed it in that way, they assumed, and we say unreasonably assumed, in paragraph 335 that P1351 was received by Bruno, speculating that P -- 3D03065 showed he was following the events in Gornji Vakuf closely. Your Honour, that kind of speculation has no place in a criminal trial where evidence has to be led to prove matters to the criminal standard. And, really, if there was a moot court, it would be a very basic argument for a first-year law student to be able to argue that particular point as far as relevance and probative value is concerned, in our respectful submission. Your Honour, this confusion of parties, and you're caught in the middle unfortunately, I'm sorry, bandering facts around, the need to be grasped, that the Trial Chamber -- clear error in relation to sniping, we've heard how the Prosecution -- the adjectives, the terrible man of Bruno Stojic and charge of sniping, well, I can understand their position in the sense they're defending a decision, a decision that we say withers under scrutiny. Because in paragraph 368 of volume 4, the majority say Bruno Stojic admitted that he controlled the snipers positioned in the glass wall bank [sic]. Well, that's wrong. He didn't admit it. And am I misrepresenting the position or is it absolutely accurate? Your Honours, in the -- bear with me a moment. Sorry, one moment, Your Honours, I do apologise. In the documents regarding sniping -- sorry, just one second. Here it is, I put it for safekeeping and forgot about it. There's an exhibit, P2806. And this is a report that was before the Chamber from the expert -- from the witness that the majority quoted and, Your Honour, it's under seal so I won't cite it in detail. But what's very clear is the particular witness who I would not name in that report dated the 16th of June, 1993, states that snipers were under full control and it goes on. Not of Bruno Stojic. Were under full control in the -- in the gymnasium. Now when that individual, I think it's public, gave evidence -- I think it's public, Mr. van der Grinten -- I think it's public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: It's public. When he gave evidence, page 21051 on the 7th of October, 2007, lines 1 to 5, and I quote the question: "Q. So Mr. Stojic himself told you that the snipers located the in these two buildings were under HVO control? He said that himself?" Answer at line 4, the witness: "Yeah, this is not my text. It the text I noted or we noted after the conversation. "Judge Antonetti: Fine. So what you're writing are Mr. Stojic's words." Answer, line 8: "That's correct." So the spin that somehow Mr. Stojic is saying snipers under his control is belied by documentary evidence which makes no mention of that and the witness himself who states Mr. Stojic says the snipers under HVO control, which is something quite different. And these are important matters because they go to so many aspects of the Prosecution's case. The Prosecution has made submissions in relation to question 8 and terror, but the sniping he is being accused of as being in charge of, the evidence found by the Chamber doesn't accord with the transcript 21051 that I've just read out in court. Your Honour, the Prosecution stated when they started that I didn't say much about Mr. Stojic. Well, that is hardly -- I think the word used is not political victim. I don't think I used those words at all. Hardly a political victim. And, Your Honour, the question of this case isn't whether somebody is an angel. It's not whether even with the benefit of hindsight morally things could have been done better, things could have been done differently. It is whether or not the Prosecution proved the case that they constructed with the vehicle of JCE that they decided upon. And we say that that is the fundamental premise that the case, the appeal must proceed upon. Now, actually, it is relevant to go into what Bruno Stojic -- because he was appointed to the head of the Defence department in July 1992. Previously he had been in charge of logistics. We said, of course, throughout that was his area of logistics, even as a minister of -- a head of defence, his job was logistics, that his previous experience is why he was selected. The majority disregarded that. They found against us. But it is important that he took up that position in July 1992 because all the pages written by the Prosecution about meetings between Milosevic and Tudjman, the meeting in Graz in Austria, the formation of the HVO, all of that is irrelevant when it comes to assessing Bruno Stojic because he wasn't even part, he wasn't even part of that Defence Department at that moment in time. Your Honours, the Prosecution have talked about Gornji Vakuf and with your leave, I just want to put on the screen two documents which are relevant for your determination. Your Honour, you will see here two extracts of the judgement. Same Judges, same majority, same volume. And in relation to Grounds 27 to 37 and the issue of Mr. Stojic's responsibility in the municipalities of which Gornji Vakuf was one, it is very interesting to note that at paragraph 329, the Judges -- the majority found that P3418, which was sent to Mr. Stojic and General Petkovic, established beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Stojic was thus informed that men who did not belong to any armed force were detained in Prozor. In relation to exactly the same document copied to Mr. Petkovic, at paragraph 799, the Judges came to precisely the opposite conclusion. They found that they couldn't establish beyond reasonable doubt that General Petkovic was informed of the fact. Two diametrically opposing interpretations, two absolutely contrary findings in relation to the same document. It cannot stand. For many reasons. Under the principle of in dubio pro reo for one, we're entitled for that document to be treated in the same way that the Judges decide it should be treated to General Petkovic. Your Honour, that's in our written brief, not responded to by the Prosecution at all. The idea that in relation to specific intent and the crimes of terror, that they must have known, should have known debate of command responsibility has somehow metamorphisised, it's morphed into this new radical concept of Judges must have meant, is something for which no authority was cited. It is such a fundamental, it is such a basic finding that is required in a decision that we say for the reasons that are detailed in our brief that the only option is to reverse the finding for the reasons that we give. Your Honours will be well familiar with your previous holdings, including in the Krajisnik case, that you shouldn't -- you would be wary to trespass into a factual determination that was within the proper purview of the court of first instance, and Your Honours then said that you would not engage in speculation. It does require speculation. Why? It requires speculation for many reasons, not only that no finding of specific intent was found, but also it relates to an expanded JCE crime in relation to Mostar so it needs to be plead specifically, with specific dates how and when those crimes came into existence. But, Your Honour, there's also clear evidence that's detailed, included by the judgment in paragraph 361 and in our brief, where the Bench reply upon - the Trial Chamber replied upon - a dinner on the 17th of July, 1993, where Bruno Stojic indicated that there was a plan to exert pressure on East Mostar in order to force, not the civilians, but the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to leave the sector. And that suggests, in my respectful submission beyond any doubt that the primary purpose was military advantage; it wasn't to terrorise. And indeed the same reference shows according, to the Judges, that Bruno Stojic offered to assist in organising the evacuation of the largest possible number of civilians from East Mostar, which we say is prima facie evidence that is completely incompatible with an intent to spread terror. In addition to that, Your Honour, there's other evidence, for example, the provision of medical supplies by Bruno Stojic which is in our brief at paragraph 316, and the fact that even the Judges accepted that between July and November the HVO attempted to manage the problem of electricity and water supplies at paragraph 1218 of the judgment. Your Honours, you can't step in to the melee of issues that the Trial Chamber should have found, that they were required to find, if there was any hope of sustaining the convictions that they entered themselves against Bruno Stojic. In the circumstance, Your Honour, it is our respectful prayer that that finding and that count is also reversed. Your Honours, we're very grateful for the time given to us. I believe that's all the time I've got; but for all the reasons detailed today and in our brief, we'd ask that the judgment be -- the convictions be overturned for the reasons given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we have two minutes which I would use for the transcript. The Prosecutor showed us today document P02608, which allegedly refers to the moving in of Croatian soldiers into apartments from which Bosniaks were expelled. Your Honours, that document does not say that at all. That is a document that speaks about the temporary moving in of members of the HVO, pursuant to a decree by the HVO. An identical decree was adopted by the B&H army about the temporary use of abandoned flats. Perhaps it's not clear to you - I don't want to testify - but when you look at it, I assert that all the persons who left those apartments were members of the Serbian army and absolutely by names you can see that there is no Muslim name there but only Serb names. There is one Muslim name of a significant person, but that person left Mostar for different reasons. Another thing, Your Honour. The Prosecution claimed here today that it is exactly true that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- or actually that the HVO helped the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but, Your Honours, this is how I wish to finish up. Could you please look in detail document 2D00311. It's a document indicated shown by my colleague. It's a document that speaks to the sending of vast quantities of arms in March 1993 to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's a document that talks about how the weapons were sent in 13 trucks, of which seven trucks were trailer trucks. This is March 1993. And when the Prosecutor persists in asserting today that the JCE began on 15th of January, how can this quantity of weapons that is without doubt being sent to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the Grude logistical base fits into that JCE? I believe, I believe that it denies that document completely. Thank you very much, Your Honours.
